title: Paul Schrader Says He Can’t Stop Writing About Guilt: “You Don’t Outrun Your Childhood”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 6:16am Paul Schrader ahead of his Venice Film Festival press conference on Sep. 4, 2026 Courtesy of Getty Paul Schrader has spent half a century writing men who sit alone in rooms , filling notebooks with confessions no one asked for. On Friday in Venice, the 79-year-old writer-director offered a simple explanation for why he has never been able to put the subject down: he was programmed early, and the program still runs. “I was raised a Dutch Calvinist, and, you know, Freud said you’re programmed by the time you’re five or six, maybe it’s even as late as eight or nine,” Schrader said at the press conference for The Basics of Philosophy , which has its world premiere Friday out of competition at the Venice Film Festival. “But anyway, once they pour that programming into you, you just run that program for the rest of your life, and no matter how far you run and how fast you run, you don’t outrun your childhood. My childhood was one of predestination, of guilt, of total depravity and all that, and, you know, Christian schools all the way through divinity school. So I don’t know how I do not write about guilt and redemption.” Related Stories Movies The 'Holy Wood Dust' Director Wants You to Know Your Christmas Tree Is a Living Being With 20 Senses Movies An Indigenous Man Navigates Identity and Desire in 'Nosotros' (Exclusive TIFF Trailer) The Basics of Philosophy stars Jack Huston as John Jorissen, a philosophy professor whose controlled, meticulously ordered life conceals a long-buried transgression. When the person he wronged unexpectedly reappears, Jorissen is thrown into a reckoning of guilt, desire and self-justification — familiar terrain for a filmmaker whose gallery of isolated, self-documenting men has included a taxi driver, a gigolo, a minister and a gardener before arriving, now, at a tenured academic. Sofia Boutella plays Becca, Jorissen’s partner and colleague in the department, with Daniel Zovatto, Bill Pullman and Dana Delany also starring, alongside Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman and Elizabeth Petruso. Martin Scorsese serves as executive producer, his second time in that role for Schrader after 2021’s The Card Counter , extending a collaboration that stretches back to Taxi Driver , Raging Bull and The Last Temptation of Christ . ‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Venice Film Festival Huston, who appears opposite Pullman as his character’s father, said what drew him to Jorissen was the absence of anything monstrous on the surface. “It’s not a portrait of the boogeyman, the man coming at you with a knife held high. It’s the person living in plain sight. It’s the everyman,” the actor said. “I thought it was a really interesting portrait of somebody who is actually struggling with a terrible part of his past, and trying to recompense this idea of: am I a monster?” Asked about a sequence in which Jorissen finds himself walking alongside a long-dead philosopher, debating whether human beings are capable of change, Huston said he had considered who he would want beside him on that walk. “If I was to take a walk with somebody, it would be possibly with my grandfather,” he said, referring to the Oscar-winning actor and director John Huston. “I have a lot of questions in life and work and all sorts. He died when I was quite young, but I’ve luckily had wonderful family members who’ve been able to share about his life and thoughts and teachings, but I think that would be a fun conversation.” Boutella, whose character is left to decide how much of her partner’s account she is willing to accept, said she deliberately withheld her own verdict on Becca. “As an actor, I hide my own answers for what she really believes,” she said. Pullman, meanwhile, delivered the conference’s biggest laugh with an account of Schrader’s casting process, which the director apparently conducts with no diplomatic padding whatsoever. “Paul’s very frank about casting. You know, usually by the time you get on the set, he’s told me several times about who they offered it to that didn’t do it,” Pullman said. “And I was glad that I was somewhere on the list, and that everybody that went before me just bowed out for various reasons.” THR

title: Netflix Hikes UK Prices, With Cheapest Plan Jumping A Third
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart French TV In Focus: Screenings & Shows To Watch At The Unifrance Rendez-Vous VodafoneThree Launching Vodafone TV In The UK, Bundling Netflix, HBO Max & Live Channels ‘Miraculous’ Studio Founder Jeremy Zag To Receive Deadline’s French TV Disruptor Award At The Unifrance Rendez-Vous View All September 4, 2026 6:02am Netflix Justin Sullivan/Getty Images It’s become pricier to watch Love Is Blind and The Gentlemen in the UK after Netflix upped its prices, hiking the monthly cost of its cheapest package by a third. The changes narrow the pricing gap between Netflix’s cheapest ad-supported tier and its top-level plan. The streamer’s new UK pricing kicked in yesterday, September 3, with little fanfare. It last put up the cost of subscribing in February. Specifically, the cost of the Standard with Ads plan has risen 33.4% from £5.99 ($8.10) to £7.99 ($10.81) a month. The price for the Standard tier is up 7.7% from £12.99 to £13.99, while Premium has gone from £18.99 to £20.99, a 10.5% uptick. Related Stories Books Everything We Know About Netflix's 'Better Than The Movies' Feature Adaptation So Far News 'Famous Last Words' Interview With Gloria Steinem Streaming Now On Netflix The pricing applies to new and existing customers. Netflix has over 18M subs in the UK. Watch on Deadline Confirming the changes to Deadline, Netflix said the price rises “reflect improvements to our wide range of entertainment and the quality of our service.” The streamer’s statement added: “Our approach remains the same: we continue offering a range of prices and plans to meet a variety of needs, and as we deliver more value to our members, we reinvest in quality entertainment and improve their experience by updating our prices.” It added: “We know members have never had more choices in entertainment, and we’re committed to delivering an experience that meets and exceeds their expectations.” It is certainly correct to say UK consumers have a wide range of free and paid-for choices for TV. The news comes in the same week that telco giant VodafoneThree announced it is rolling out Vodafone TV, a new service launching in October that sees free channels bundled with Netflix and HBO Max, and which will also offer access to AVOD services such as Tubi. title: Cédric Kahn Talks Exploration Of Youth Mental Health Issues In Venice Contender ‘A Place To Heal’ + Trailer: “There’s More Hope With Adolescents”
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 6:00am 'A Place To Heal' Ad Vitam French director Cédric Kahn hits the Venice Film Festival’s this evening with Golden Lion contender A Place To Heal (15/18) set against the backdrop of an adolescent psychiatric ward. It promises to be one of this Venice’s most youthful red carpets as the director is joined by the dozen young actors at the heart of the production in which he also co-stars as the head psychiatrist of the unit. “They’re all very excited and I’m very happy about it because I’ve attended a lot of films festivals in my time but to experience a festival through their eyes will be a pleasure,” says Kahn, who has a long history with Venice having shown his first feature Railway Bar in its parallel Critics’ Week sidebar in 1992, returning in 2023 with Making of in its official selection. The youthful excitement will be an antidote to a tough but hopeful film digging into the issue of adolescent mental health issues. The young subjects include Lucia (Malou Khebizi) a tough-talking runaway, old beyond her years, who was abused by a stepfather as a child; Éloïse (Zoé Monpart), a seemingly privileged kid, suffering from eating disorders and depression who gradually opens up about the cause of her pain; Marvin (Daoud Gary), who is interned after a sudden psychotic episode, and Enzo (Kenji Peyran), a streetwise tearaway with a history of abandonment as a child, whose arrival on the ward upsets its fragile equilibrium. Deadline can reveal a first clip below giving a sense of the ward and its highs and lows, as the staff sets about the task of healing their young patients. “I’ve wanted to make a film about psychiatry for a very long time. It was a date with destiny for me. I’ve often explored mental fragility in my previous films; so, to make a film on this subject was a long-standing appointment,” explains Kahn about the origin of the film. The director had false starts as he tried to figure out how to explore the subject on the big screen. “I worked on an initial project a few years back that focused more on adult psychiatry, specifically from the perspective of the medical staff,” he recounts. “The film’s protagonist was a psychiatrist, but I wasn’t happy with the script, so I completely changed my approach to the subject; approaching it through the lens of adolescents felt more positive to me… there’s more hope with adolescents.” The young psychiatric patients in A Place to Heal are based on research carried out by co-writer Kahina Le Querrec, who spent six months immersed in a child and adolescent psychiatry unit, while Kahn also gained personal insight through three weeks spent in a unit in Paris. “She gathered the children’s accounts and spoke with the psychiatrists and medical staff, and we wrote the screenplay based on that material… they are all true stories, re-enacted by other adolescents.” Kahn acknowledges that one of the themes running through the drama is the role parents in their children’s mental health issues. “There are many contexts, but obviously, family and parents play a major role in children’s dysfunction,” says Kahn. “I know that for parents, the film can create a sense of unease or guilt… I have friends who saw the film who told me they were asking themselves throughout the film whether they were bad parents.” The film comes at a time of reports of a growing health crisis amongst youngsters, in the wake of the Covid-19pandemic and the rise of smart phones and social media. Kahn questions whether is a rise in mental health problems, suggesting rather than it has become more acceptable to talk about mental health issues openly, adding the supposed trend was not at the heart of his intentions for the film. “I wanted to show that when it comes to psychological or psychiatric issues, it’s actually a very democratic experience. We’re all on equal footing. And then, there are also issues that are truly timeless,” he says. “While I do somewhat call out the role of parents, I’m not really criticizing a specific era in the film. I don’t dwell much on eco-anxiety or Covid. We tried to make a film that feels fairly timeless. It’s not a judgment on the times, not at all, but it is a judgment on the family; that’s for sure.” “The issue of family is something that runs through all my films. The topic of parent control, I’ve addressed it in every film; it’s a continuation of that theme. So, I’d say that’s more my personal subject matter than the topic of psychiatry itself.” Related Stories News Theo Rollason On How He Discovered 30 Hours Of Behind-The-Scenes Derek Jarman Footage To Create 'Queer Edward II' -- Venice News International Insider: Ciao, Venice; 'Bake Off' Battle Heats Up; Leslie Odom Jr. Chat The film is produced by Ad Vitam Films, which will release the film in France on November 18, in coproduction with Kahn’s Trop de Bonheur Productions and France 2 Cinéma. Charades handles international sales. title: Formula 1’s Next Big Bet: A Live Entertainment Event in Milan
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 6:00am Kane Brown performs on stage during F1 75 Live at The O2 Arena on February 18, 2025 in London, England. Photo by Zak Mauger/Getty Images Formula 1 is planning a multi-day event “spectacular” early next year, in a bid to hype up racing fans and bring new viewers into the tent. The event will be called F1 Live Milan, and will be held in Milan, Italy Feb. 18-20. While specifics are still being hashed out, it will include a fan fest that will be held over the course of the three days, with a headlining event called F1 The Show, which will include appearances from all of F1’s drivers and team principals, as well as live music and entertainment. F1 previously held a live event in London in 2025, tied to the sport’s 75th anniversary, but the racing circuit, which has a media deal with Apple TV in the U.S., is planning an even bigger venture for the new installment. F1 remains an emerging sport in the U.S., and the new event, which will stream globally, is part of the push to grow the sport’s fanbase stateside, even as it engages fans elsewhere around the world. Among other moves, the circuit, which is owned by John Malone’s Liberty Media, added a new U.S. team in Cadillac earlier this year. There are also a number of North American races on the annual calendar, including in Austin, Texas, Montreal, Mexico City, and of course the high-profile races in Miami and Las Vegas, where F1 is establishing a year-round experiential space. “We are always thinking big and pushing boundaries, and F1 Live Milan is going to be an incredible experience created with our fans at its heart,” Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali said in a statement. “We want them to feel that they are not simply watching the sport, but they are truly immersed in it. It is an important part of our ongoing ambition to bring Formula 1 closer to fans than ever before, giving them the chance to see their heroes up close and experience the energy, innovation, and emotion that make Formula 1 so unique. As F1 continues to reach new audiences around the world, racing will always be our soul but we also want to create unforgettable experiences that bring the excitement of Formula 1 to life on an even bigger scale and continue to explore what is possible. “Building on the extraordinary success of F1 75 in London, F1 Live Milan will transform the city into a Formula 1 festival for three unforgettable days, bringing people together from across the globe to celebrate everything they love about our sport,” he added. “I know my fellow Italians will offer a fantastic welcome to fans traveling to F1 Live Milan and I cannot wait to see the city come to life with Formula 1 energy, creating memories that will last a lifetime.” THR

title: Theo Rollason On How He Discovered 30 Hours Of Behind-The-Scenes Derek Jarman Footage To Create ‘Queer Edward II’ — Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Gets Rapturous 14-Minute Standing Ovation At Venice World Premiere Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Earns Five-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere ‘The Fastest Man In The World’: Biopic Of Four-Time Paralympic Gold Medalist Tony Volpentest In The Works View All September 4, 2026 5:59am Theo Rollason Aurore Marechal/Getty Images. In 1991, British filmmaker Derek Jarman screened Edward II, his political and wildly inventive adaptation of Christopher Marlowe’s classic play, at the Venice Film Festival. The film was a hit with critics, and Tilda Swinton, who starred alongside Steven Waddington and Andrew Tiernan, won the festival’s Best Actress award. This week, exactly 35 years later, Edward II returns to the Lido in the form of a brilliant behind-the-scenes documentary about the film’s eventful production from first-time filmmaker Theo Rollason . The documentary is titled Queer Edward II and screens this afternoon in an Out Of Competition slot on the Lido. Related Stories News Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: "I've Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings" Festivals Jack Huston On The Tough Questions About Sexual Abuse Posed By Paul Schrader's Film 'The Basics Of Philosophy': "It's Almost Become A Taboo Subject" - Venice Film Festival An assortment of former Jarman acolytes, such as Swinton and Sandy Powell, are Executive Producers on the project alongside other interesting names like Christine Vachon and Russell Tovey. Seamus McGarvey, the Irish DoP behind titles like Joe Wright’s Atonement , Tom Ford’s Nocturnal Animals , and Lynne Ramsay’s We Need to Talk About Kevin, is credited as the cinematographer. The film has been pieced together using footage that a young McGarvey, then fresh into his career behind a camera, shot on the Edward II set. Watch on Deadline “It was all just sitting in a cupboard for 35 years,” Rollason says of the footage, which he stumbled upon after a tip from a friend. Alongside editor Nicole Hálová, Rollason began the lengthy process of combing through the hours of footage, and he has carved out an illuminating portrait not only of Jarman’s unique artistic practice but also of his much-less-talked-about leadership in the gay rights movement in the UK. Producers on the title are Ben Fowlie, Sebastien Rabas, and Michael Sherman. Simon Fisher Turner composed the score, and Dora Ash Sakula and Neo Michael were the archival producers. After Venice, Queer Edward II will screen at the London Film Festival. Below, Rollason speaks with Deadline in depth about the miraculous story behind his discovery of McGarvey’s footage, starting the project completely independently with no funding, and how he hopes the film can “form a little companion piece” to Jarman’s Edward II . Venice runs until September 12. DEADLINE: Theo, how did you find this footage? THEO ROLLASON: It’s an odd story. So Derek was making Edward II , and Sarah Swords, who’d worked on The Garden with Derek, wanted to make a behind-the-scenes film about Edward II . She hired Seamus McGarvey, who’d also worked on The Garden , and sent him on his way with a camera. At the end of production, as often happens with these kinds of indie productions, Seamus turned up and said, “Here’s the footage,” and they said, “We don’t have any money.” So the footage ended up with Ahmad Ahmadzadeh, who runs the camera company that hired out the camera to Seamus. And it was all just sitting in a cupboard for 35 years. I’ve known Ahmad for years, and he got in touch with me because I’ve worked as an archivist previously and said, “Can you give me your opinion on this material?” He knew I liked Derek Jarman’s films, and watching it was incredible. It was a real look behind the production and who Derek was. The final step in realizing this could be a feature film was that the politics of the time were really thoroughly explored on the set. I spent a while convincing Ahmad that there was a feature film here, and not just the typical behind-the-scenes featurette. DEADLINE: How much footage was there? Was it reels? ROLLASON: 30 hours of Betacam SP. There could have been a watchable 15-hour film in the footage. All credit to Seamus. He was in his early to mid-20s when he shot this. He wasn’t strictly a documentary filmmaker, but he’s just so intuitive with a camera. He’s constantly finding the right expressions to cut away to. It’s really the easiest job in the world watching his rushes because it’s basically been edited in camera. Theo Rollason’s ‘ Queer Edward II ‘. Lightborn Films. DEADLINE: What did Seamus say when you first contacted him with the idea? ROLLASON: He was surprised. No one knew that the footage still existed. Everyone had forgotten about it or assumed it was gone. So when we originally got in touch with him and asked whether he would be okay with us making this film, he was just delighted. For him, it was emotional to see one of the very first projects he worked on, which he had thought had come to nothing, being brought back to life. DEADLINE: Watching this film and seeing Derek at length, you realize how English he was. I’d never really thought of him in that context. ROLLASON: Yes, and that was one of the other appeals of the material: it couldn’t be more British and specifically English. Just the way he speaks, but also all the stuff he’s interested in talking about. The first scene we put in the film shows Derek talking about Marks and Spencer’s underwear, and that sets the tone. It’s an amazing document of the UK at that time. DEADLINE: So much gets lost when a person dies, and there’s all this mythmaking about who they were. In Derek’s case, I feel like people don’t really consider how involved he was in the gay rights movement. ROLLASON: Yeah, that was the breakthrough for me. There are obviously a few films about Derek Jarman. There’s Isaac Julien’s film, which does a great job of telling his life story. And within that, his involvement with the gay rights protest group OutRage. I knew Derek’s films very well, but I wasn’t as aware of just how directly politically involved he was. It’s fairly obvious from Edward II where his politics lie, but that doesn’t really give you the sense that he was on the streets with OutRage. He wasn’t watching from afar and making these comments. He was really doing it from the inside. And basically, all the archive footage in the film that isn’t on the set of Edward II is there to give that context. DEADLINE: Filmmaking is always hard. But this is a unique project. Was it tough to raise funds and get people on board? ROLLASON: It was incredibly easy to get people emotionally on board. The goodwill around Derek’s legacy is unbelievable. I don’t think many subjects could garner the kind of response Derek gets from people. Financing, obviously, is a different thing, and we did it probably the most insane way we could have, which was starting production without any financing, which was a huge leap of faith, especially as a first-time filmmaker. I’m not sure I’d ever do it again. I’ve made shorts before, but I haven’t made documentaries. I didn’t really have anything to prove myself, so there was an element of, if I just start making this film and we have something to show people, then, you know, fingers crossed, the money will follow. And it took a while, but it eventually did. DEADLINE: What’s your background? How did you start making films? ROLLASON: I’ve worked as a film critic for years. I love writing about film. And everything I’ve learned about film has been from watching an obscene amount of films. I didn’t go to film school or anything like that. I’ve always wanted to make films, but didn’t have the confidence. Over the last few years, I taught myself how to edit at a job I had producing video content. I did some video essay stuff. I put out a short film, which was very loosely narrative or experimental. I also worked as an archivist for the estate of the artist Paula Rego, and got very interested in large film and photo archives. DEADLINE: Is that footage at the end of the film where Derek is at a screening from Venice? ROLLASON: It is. He was there showing Blue at the Biennale a couple of months before he died. That footage is amazing. He’s so obviously very unwell by that point, but he writes about it so warmly in his diaries, and it felt like a really lovely glimpse into the future. I was a bit concerned that, in trying to make a film set on the Edward II set, I would give the impression that it was Derek’s last film. That’s why I wanted to have this flash-forward, to show that that wasn’t the case, but also to hit home that this was quite close to his death. DEADLINE: How does it feel to now be showing your film at Venice? ROLLASON: It’s crazy. The reason we started the film with no funding was that we looked at the submission dates for Venice. It’s 35 years ago this week that Edward II played Venice, and we just thought, that’s a really neat little thing; should we go for it? If I’m honest, I didn’t think there was any chance that this film would be here. It’s completely surreal. DEADLINE: How would you like this film to be viewed? I couldn’t help but think of the many possibilities to distribute it. It could go along with a retrospective of Derek’s many works, for example. ROLLASON: I would love for it to be shown with Edward II as much as possible. If this film is a chance for Derek’s films to be seen more widely, that’s always great. But Edward II, especially, is such a special film, and it hasn’t been seen as widely, certainly in the UK, in the last decade. I hope this can form a little companion piece to Edward II . Beyond that, I’m excited to see how it lands with a British audience. title: Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei, in Venice With ‘Falling House,’ Set to Shoot ‘Centrifugal Force’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 5:43am PT Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei, in Venice With ‘Falling House,’ Set to Shoot ‘Centrifugal Force’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei, in Venice With ‘Falling House,’ Set to Shoot ‘Centrifugal Force’ (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago Anna Foglietta on Working With Alba Rohrwacher on Venice Drama ‘A Common Story’ ‘You Have to Have the Guts to Show Yourself Exactly as You Are’ — Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Venice Market Chief Pascal Diot Says He’s Not Affected by New Toronto Market: ‘Not What the Industry Wants Now’ 8 hours ago See All Courtesy Seven Springs Pictures Iranian director Mohsen Gharaei, who is at the Venice Film Festival with well-received drama “Falling House,” is set to shoot a new film titled “Centrifugal Force” that will capture “the impossible choices facing a generation of Iranians today,” as the synopsis puts it. “Falling House,” which world-premiered on Wed. in Venice’s Orizzonti sidebar, follows a modest family on the outskirts of Tehran who faces the imminent destruction of their home as part of a vast redevelopment project. Rashid, the patriarchal father and a prison guard, attempts to contain family rebellion while being accused of corruption. Related Stories Jessica Simpson Doc Set at Netflix From ‘Robbie Williams’ Director Joe Pearlman (EXCLUSIVE) 'Scooby-Doo' Netflix Series Casts Andre Benjamin, Cathy Moriarty “Centrifugal Force,” which will be shot in an undisclosed location outside Iran in Farsi and English with still unspecified Iranian and international actors, will be “a deeply human story about what happens when the home you love is no longer a place you can return to,” Gharaei said in his directors’ statement. Popular on Variety “After finishing my latest film, I found myself on an unexpected journey from one geography to another,” Gharaei, who is now living as an exile outside Iran, added. “But migration is not simply a matter of moving from one place to another; it is a moment when a person is suddenly pushed out of the center of their own life. The journey becomes most painful when departure is not a choice, when all familiar paths close, one by one, and suddenly you have to leave a home that you still love.” “Centrifugal Force” will be the story of a family that has remained in Iran for years, not entirely out of contentment, but out of the hope that somehow it might still be possible to build a life with all its contradictions. They have held onto staying and created a sense of order for themselves within a system they believed to be stable. But in a geography like Iran, where the line between simply surviving and truly living can shift without notice, no sense of order is ever completely safe,” Gharaei went on to note. “With forced migration, the family enters a world governed by a different set of rules, where things no longer work as they used to. What appears from the outside to be a form of escape can, from within, feel like a kind of collapse. Distance from home makes the distance between family members visible. It reopens old wounds. Crisis challenges the image they have of one another. It is as if migration does not only change their physical location; it also displaces their understanding of home, family, and even self,” he continued. “This is where centrifugal force takes shape, drawing people away from a point to which they have been deeply attached, without necessarily knowing what lies ahead. Within this deracination, the family is as weightless as hay, easily pulled away from the center. And the further they move from it, the more they are confronted with the question of what truly connected them in the first place: geography, memory, habit, or something else for which they have no name.” Just like “Falling House,” “Centrifugal Force” is being produced by Iranian producer Milad Khosravi through his Seven Springs Pictures company in tandem with Oscar-winning producer Odessa Rae (“Navalny,” “The Voice of Hind Rajab”). title: The ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Director Wants You to Know Your Christmas Tree Is a Living Being With 20 Senses
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 5:30am 'Holy Wood Dust' Courtesy of Be Water Film Director Victor Kossakovsky has developed a reputation for making us reevaluate how we think about human and more-than-human life. His emotional and tender Gunda (2020), about a pig and her piglets, was the first film in his “empathy trilogy.” Last year, his Trillion , a wordless documentary following an artist returning fish scales to the ocean in Norway, was a reference to the estimated number of fish taken from the world’s oceans by humans every year. At the Venice Film Festival , Kossakovsky will world premiere, in a Venice Open – Out of Competition slot on Sept. 6, his new film, Holy Wood Dust , a cinematic invitation into the life and world of trees in collaboration with Italian botanist and author Stefano Mancuso – and an invitation to change our perspective. Related Stories Movies An Indigenous Man Navigates Identity and Desire in 'Nosotros' (Exclusive TIFF Trailer) Lifestyle Maggie Gyllenhaal's Venice Film Festival Style “While art may be powerless to halt the conflicts unfolding around us and cannot stop the bullets of today, I believe that telling stories rooted in empathy can plant the seeds for a more peaceful future,” the Russian-born Kossakovsky says in a director’s statement on the Venice website. “What happens to a stump the second after a tree is cut down? What does that tree think and feel at that very moment?” a synopsis for the film asks. “ Holy Wood Dust is an invitation to radically reimagine the plant kingdom from a new, groundbreaking perspective.” Holy Wood Dust comes from production companies Be Water Film, Solaria Film, RAI Cinema, Oceanika, Allegra Films and Doppelplusultra Filmproduktion. Be Water Film is handling Italian distribution, with RAI Cinema handling sales. Director Kossakovsky co-wrote the film with Mancuso. Gianmarco Donaggio is the cinematographer, with editing handled by Ainara Vera. Ahead of the film’s world premiere at Venice, THR talked to Kossakovsky about the inspiration for Holy Wood Dust , a scene that will remind cinema buffs of a Federico Fellini classic, and why he isn’t done with his “empathy” films. Why did you want to make a film about trees? When I was a kid, I walked with my mom, and I took one leaf from a bush, and my mom said: “Why did you do that?” And I said, “Oh, it’s beautiful.” And she said, “If we take out one of your hairs, do you feel pain?” So I said, “Yes, of course.” My mother said: “The bush feels the same. It feels pain. So don’t do that any longer.” This has stayed with me all my life. Once I lived in Berlin, there was a brilliant autumn, and I picked up a dead leaf that had fallen off a tree. I broke it in front of a microscope, and I saw something unbelievable. You know what happens to us if you cut your finger? Blood is trying to heal and close the [wound], right? And that made me wonder: What if I looked through a microscope when they cut a tree? What would I see? Of course, it’s complicated, and you cannot bring a microscope to the forest. So, making a film [about this] was a challenge. But we finally made it, and it really looks like War and Peace . You can see that this tree is totally confused [when things shown in the film happen to the region it stands in]. The tree has lived for 100 years, so what suddenly happened? I remember I was filming and shaking because it’s obvious that something bad happened to the tree, something horrible. It’s confused, suffering, trying to heal and trying to fight. How did you end up collaborating on Holy Wood Dust with Stefano Mancuso? My assistant was reading something from him during another project when we were on a boat in a storm. She told me, “You have to read this!” So, I started to read it and then had to buy more of his books, and then I wrote him. And a miracle happened. He wrote back to me in one minute: “I saw a few of your films, so I want to see you as well.” So, it happened by coincidence that we both needed each other. He is a visionary man. And 15 years ago, I started thinking about this film. ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Courtesy of Be Water Film Did you always know it would be a film about fir trees? I had a few different ideas, a few different characters. At first, it was supposed to be a film about linden trees [or basswood trees, as they are known in the U.S.]. They are very cinematic. They are like this. (He stretches his arms to the sides.) With a Christmas tree, it’s just a vertical triangle, which is not cinematic, especially in the film format I like. I like the 2:1 aspect ratio, which makes things very difficult for a Christmas tree. But I said no, I need to find something to challenge myself with a tree, which doesn’t look good in this aspect ratio, and it needed to be something universal. And Christmas is, of course, something everyone is attached to emotionally. We kind of all connect to the idea of Christmas, and so I decided to make a film for kids and for families. There is an iconic-feeling scene in Holy Wood Dust of a helicopter flying a Christmas tree towards the Vatican. Am I right to see that as a conscious reference to Federico Fellini’s La Dolce Vita , which has that famous scene of a helicopter above Rome transporting a statue of Jesus Christ to the Vatican? I really wanted to say my thanks to Fellini because I remember the moment when I first saw one of his films. I was a teenager, and I saw 8½ in a very good cinema in Saint Petersburg. I remember when the film finished, people left, and I was alone, crying, and I wouldn’t stop. I was just crying, crying, and cleaning ladies came in and started to brush, and they looked at me and said, “Okay, cry, my friend, cry.” It was a full cinema, but I knew the film was for me. It felt like the screen was just for me, and the film stayed with me all my life. ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Courtesy of Be Water Film There is also a powerful scene in the film where Stefano Mancuso and a group of kids discuss the importance and value of trees, which has surprising and impactful information. Yes, [that was] important [because] we consider trees like decoration, right? I took [some experiences] with trees as a sign to do this film. It was like a tree was crying, asking me: “Victor, see it. Do it because no one understands. Everyone considers us as decoration. We are not. We are living beings.” I find the title intriguing. Was Holy Wood Dust always the title for this film? It is great, but I’m never happy with the working title. The working title was Tears for Fears . Gunda and Trillion , both executive-produced by Joaquin Phoenix, were the first two films in what you have described as a trilogy on empathy. This film is different, as it isn’t wordless and black-and-white, but it still covers empathy. What’s your plan for the trilogy at this point? There are going to be more, at least two more. But I can’t say more at this point. ‘Holy Wood Dust’ Courtesy of Be Water Film What’s your hope for Holy Wood Dust once audiences see it? I’m not saying, Don’t celebrate Christmas, don’t have a Christmas tree! I’m saying you can do whatever you want to do, but be aware that this is not decoration. The Christmas tree is a living being. It’s a live organism, which has 20 senses, and which can live, if you don’t cut it, for 500 years. We have five senses. Plants have 20 senses, at least 20. Imagine that, and then you can do whatever you want. You can cut a tree, put it in your corner, and then you can throw it away. Just be aware that if you don’t cut it, it can live for 500 years. But this film, I believe, kids will love, and families will love because, in a way, it’s a Christmas carol. THR

title: George Clooney Says the Government Shouldn’t Regulate AI: ‘These Are Not the People You Want to Entrust the Holy Grail With’
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 5:09am PT George Clooney Says the Government Shouldn’t Regulate AI: ‘These Are Not the People You Want to Entrust the Holy Grail With’ By Elsa Keslassy , K.J. Yossman Getty George Clooney has said he doesn’t trust the government to regulate AI. “I don’t know that you want government to be regulating this either, because I sit and watch when Zuckerberg is testifying in front of, you know, a 94-year-old Chuck Grassley, and they’re like, ‘Well, how do you turn that computer on?’” he joked, before adding, “These are not the people that you want to entrust the holy grail with.” Related Stories ‘The Gentlemen’ Officially Renewed for Season 3 as First Season 2 Trailer Drops: ‘I’m Looking Forward to Pushing the Boundaries Further,’ Guy Ritchie Says (EXCLUSIVE) 'Emomee,' Indian Kids Life-Skills Series, Lands on Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) Clooney, who was speaking at a Venice Film Festival symposium hosted by CAA and Finch & Partners, joined the panel on the future of creativity alongside diverse figures including artist Kennedy Yanko, filmmaker Giuseppe Tornator, clergyman Cardinal José Tolentino de Mendonça and National Gallery of Art president Darren Walker. Popular on Variety The actor said AI was dangerous because it could make people doubt about real things, as well as invent things that don’t exist. “It’s not just that you’ll see lies,” he said. “It also makes you question things that really do exist. It also that sort of world of fake news — suddenly you’re able to take things that really happened and say, ‘Well, that didn’t happen either.” “You’ll have people who deny the Holocaust, and that will have the same weight in AI as facts.” Clooney also talked about how his wife Amal Clooney, a prominent human rights lawyer, has come across laws that were invented by AI. They “will hallucinate and make up fake cases, and lawyers who don’t check it will quote those cases, or judges will quote those cases,” he warned. “I think that’s some of the danger in all of this, is that we’re looking at something going, ‘We’re not sure where this is going to end, and we’re not sure who’s fully in charge,” he said, adding that these AI tools are owned by “richest people in the world.” The risks presented by deep fakes could also lead to real-life consequences aside from disinformation. “That’s a joke for people, but what happens when you see a video of Putin saying he’s launched the first nuclear strike in the United States? And how do you discern it?” Talking about his hopes for the next presidential election and for potential candidates, Clooney said, “We’re all very excited by this young senator from Georgia named Jon Ossoff. We’re all excited about Jimmy [J.B.] Pritzker. I’m from Kentucky, I like Andy Beshear as a governor.” “We need young voices in there that are coming up with some new ideas and some new thoughts,” he added. Clooney also stressed the “need to have a check and balance — We’re not supposed to agree. That’s the whole idea of democracy.” Miley Cyrus Drops Last Name, Prompting Dad Billy Ray to Publicly Defend the Change: ‘Family Means More Than Ever Now’ Miley Cyrus Leads a Steamy Dance Floor Revolution With New Single and Video for ‘Bass Persuades’ Miley Cyrus Honors Godmother Dolly Parton: ‘I Have an Angel by My Side. title: An Indigenous Man Navigates Identity and Desire in ‘Nosotros’ (Exclusive TIFF Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 5:05am 'Nosotros' Courtesy of FiGa Films You have heard that moving from the countryside to the city can be challenging? Well, you haven’t met Romero, an Indigenous man in Guatemala, yet! Now, you can – and go on an intimate cinematic journey with him in Nosotros . And you can experience how he navigates identity, class, and desire after moving from the highlands to the capital of Guatemala City. Romero experiences much change in the restrained and atmospheric portrait of modern-day connection and belonging from Guatemalan producer Joaquín Ruano ( Our Mothers ) in his feature directorial debut. The film will have its world premiere on Sept. 12 in the Discovery program of the Toronto International Film Festival ( TIFF ). Related Stories Lifestyle Maggie Gyllenhaal's Venice Film Festival Style Movies 'Balcanica': When Music Is Outlawed in Afghanistan, a Conductor and His Son Must Leave All Behind (Exclusive Venice Trailer) After leaving his Indigenous family for work in Guatemala City, security guard Romero (Josef Coxaj) faces not only an unfamiliar environment, estrangement, loneliness and a “performative macho milieu,” explains a synopsis on the TIFF website. He falls for Nubia (Lola Vásquez), a transgender small business owner at the mall he patrols, “discovering an unexpected refuge and a new sense of self in a world not yet ready to make space for them.” Mayra Salvador also features in the cast. The movie also touches on the lingering scars of Guatemala’s civil war. The press notes describe Nosotros as “an intimate portrait of two people finding connection within a society where racism, transphobia, economic inequality, and deeply entrenched ideas of masculinity determine whose lives – and whose desires – are allowed space.” Ruano wrote and directed Nosotros , which features cinematography by Paolo Girón and editing by César Díaz. FiGa Films is handling sales. THR can now exclusively premiere the trailer for Nosotros ahead of its TIFF world premiere. Whenever you are ready, follow Romero on his trip to the city and into his new job, his meeting with Nubia and the start of their tender journey together. THR

(Photo by Benjamin Cremel/Getty Images) Maggie Gyllenhaal has a history on the red carpet at the Venice Film Festival. She made her first appearance on the Lido back in 2004 for the world premiere of Gregory Jacobs’ Criminal , in which she starred opposite John C. Reilly, Jonathan Tucker and Diego Luna. She followed it up a year later to support her brother, Jake, at the festival premiere of his Brokeback Mountain. Gyllenhaal didn’t come back again until 2021, but then in a different capacity as a filmmaker by bringing the world premiere of her directorial debut, The Lost Daughter , starring Olivia Colman, Dakota Johnson, Jessie Buckley and her husband Peter Sarsgaard. She left as a winner as the film earned Gyllenhaal a prize for best screenplay. Related Stories Movies 'Balcanica': When Music Is Outlawed in Afghanistan, a Conductor and His Son Must Leave All Behind (Exclusive Venice Trailer) Movies 'My Undesirable Friends: Part II -- Exile' Review: War Rages On, as Does the Journalistic Resistance, in an Essential Chronicle of Reporters Under Fire “It was really seen in Venice, and it was really appreciated in Venice,” she told Vogue of the film’s reception here. “So I will always love Venice, aside from the fact that it’s an incredible city.” After turning out another high-profile directing effort with last year’s The Bride , Venice welcomed Gyllenhaal back to the Lido to serve as president of the competition jury . She also has a project in Venice this year with her Marilyn Monroe-inspired advertorial short Flesh Impact , starring Johnson, Ellen Burstyn and Sarsgaard. The short film will screen out of competition later in the event. During such a busy run here for Gyllenhaal, it’s prime time to take a look back at her high-profile red carpet outings in Venice, showings that include a lot of Miu Miu, a little Celine, a few black-and-white ensembles, some sharp tailoring and a few head-turning high jewelry accessories. title: ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 4:24am PT ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018 By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018 2 hours ago Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Oasis Documentary Directors on Filming the Brothers’ First Reunion in 15 Years and Why There Wasn’t Much Emotion in the Room: ‘It’s the Gallaghers, It’s Not ‘Dawson’s Creek” 7 hours ago See All Everett Collection The U.K. may have just had the hottest August since records began but, in more positive news, it also had the hottest August at the box office in almost a decade. Thanks to the incredible performances of both “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “ The Odyssey ” a total of $161.3 million was earned at the box office that month, according to new figures from Rentrak, the highest since 2018’s record-breaking August with $201.7 million. Related Stories 'Emily in Paris' Season 6 First Look Shows a Glamorous Greek Adventure as Netflix Sets Christmas Release 'One Piece' Season 3 Casts Its Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka Of course, three recent years were hit by the pandemic and its impact on production, with 2020’s August sitting at a paltry $22 million, 2021’s at $87.9 million and 2022’s at $85.4 million. But as the world burned outside, this year’s bumper summer was clearly a major relief for cinemas and the industry at large as it still looks to recover following recent seismic shifts. Popular on Variety (Comscore’s official numbers do state that 2024’s August reached $163.1 million and 2019’s $167.9, those were counted as five-week periods as the company’s months run from the first Friday to the last.) “The Odyssey,” which released July 17, ended August with U.K. earnings of $108.6 million, easily Christopher Nolan’s most successful film on home soil by some margin and still number 2 in the box office after seven weeks. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” meanwhile, released on July 29 and, five weeks on, still sits atop the box office with total earnings of $126.8 million. It’ll likely top “Spider-Man: No Way Home” ($131. 7 million) as the highest-earning Marvel film in the U.K. by the end of September. Of course, the U.K. hasn’t been the only market to benefit from the colossal earnings of the two biggest films of the year so far. Even after just a few weeks in the box office, on Aug 10 they had helped the U.S. hit the summer milestone of $4 billion domestically for only the second time in the post-pandemic era. title: ‘Balcanica’: When Music Is Outlawed in Afghanistan, a Conductor and His Son Must Leave All Behind (Exclusive Venice Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 4:00am 'Balcanica' Courtesy of Nightswim Nicola Sorcinelli is exploring timely, complex and emotional issues in his feature directorial debut, Balcanica , for which THR can exclusively premiere a first teaser trailer ahead of its world premiere in the Venice Days , or Giornate degli Autori, competition, the independent sidebar of the Venice Film Festival , later on Friday. “A human story of choice and moral complexity, the film follows conductor Nazar and his son Jalil as their path crosses with Greta, an Italian doctor, and each is confronted with a decision that will change their life,” press notes highlight. Related Stories Movies 'My Undesirable Friends: Part II -- Exile' Review: War Rages On, as Does the Journalistic Resistance, in an Essential Chronicle of Reporters Under Fire Movies 'Oasis' Asks Uncomfortable Questions About Exclusion, and Its Director Explains Why Violence Is "Like a Virus" Sorcinelli’s movie stars Matilda De Angelis ( The Undoing , Fuori , The Law According to Lidia Poët ) and Berlin Silver Bear winner Babak Karimi ( A Separation ). Ivar Wafaei and Giovanni Toscano also feature in the cast. “When music is outlawed in Afghanistan, the orchestra conductor Nazar and his tuba-playing son Jalil are forced to leave everything behind,” reads a synopsis for Balcanica . “Their journey along the Balkan route toward Italy is uncertain, yet it carries the hope of finding a place where they can play again. Along the way, they meet Greta, an Italian doctor. Together, the three navigate choices that will change all of their lives.” Sorcinelli wrote the script with Andrea Brusa. The cinematography was handled by Damjan Radovanović, with Ian Degrassi serving as the editor. The movie is produced by Nightswim and Wildside, a Fremantle company, in co-production with This and That Productions and Antitalent, in association with M74 and Nieminen Film. m-appeal is in charge of world sales, with Fandango distributing the film in Italy. “ Balcanica is rooted in a lifelong anger at the ways freedom can be withheld, controlled or silenced,” Sorcinelli shares. “I grew up listening to my grandmother’s memories of fighting for freedom in the 1940s, and those stories have profoundly shaped my imagination. Years later, news of music being banned in Afghanistan – something I was too young to fully understand at the time – remained with me.” He continues: “Together with Andrea Brusa, I wanted to explore that wound through Nazar and Jalil, an Afghan father and son whose shared life as musicians becomes a journey of endurance, loss and resistance. Greta embodies the Western perspective through which this story is observed. At the heart of the film is the body: the one thing that can carry us forward, withstand cold, heat and fear, and bear the lasting marks of violence, abuse and rejection as it crosses borders.” Before you watch the exclusive trailer for Balcanica below, get ready for epic images, human drama and, of course, music. And keep in mind: “Just don’t get too attached.” THR

title: Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings”
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 3:55am May el-Toukhy Søren Rønholt May el-Toukhy is in competition at the Venice Film Festival with post-World War Two psychological thriller Woman Unknown as one of just two female directors in the running for the Golden Lion this year. Set in Denmark in the summer of 1945, the picture revolves around nanny and housemaid Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is on the cusp of marrying her wealthy, older, widowed employer (Carsten Bjørnlund). Amid the jubilation, there is a darker side to the liberation as women who fraternized with German soldiers are tracked down and publicly shamed. A painful secret from Marie’s past threatens her imminent but fragile social ascension and she will stop at nothing to prevent it from being revealed. Related Stories Festivals Jack Huston On The Tough Questions About Sexual Abuse Posed By Paul Schrader's Film 'The Basics Of Philosophy': "It's Almost Become A Taboo Subject" - Venice Film Festival News Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc 'Be Brave': "We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us" - Venice Mathilde Arcel as Marie in Woman Unknown Nordisk Film Production When Venice announced its lineup last July, el-Toukhy was the only woman in the main competition alongside 19 men. She has since been joined by Rachel Szor, co-director with Yuval Abraham of late addition Neza . Watch on Deadline It was a surprising move for a festival, which has feted three female directors with its top Golden Lion prize since 2020, and left many woman across the film industry wondering whether the drive for gender equality born out of the MeToo era was a mirage. El-Toukhy tells Deadline that while she is “delighted” and “honored” to be in competition, the lack of other women in the running for the Golden Lion this year has weighed on her since. “It tells us there’s still lots of work to do,” she says. “I think it’s very, very much a structural problem that I myself have lots of experience with. I’ve been the only woman in many, many settings.” “Going all the way back to when we get out of film school film as female filmmakers, to getting our first film done, and getting our second film done, the budgets we work under, and even sometimes the actors that say yes and the actors that say no,” she continues. “The way the media creates stories around male directors as geniuses… I’ve never heard a female director being called a genius. “We’re all part of this structure and it’s just been on my mind since how severe this problem is and how structural it is. It’s as old as cinema and even older than that. And of course, my film also speaks about some of these matters, such as the invisibility of women, in a historical context.” From Reformation Witch Hunts To Post-WW2 Purges Woman Unknown is el-Toukhy’s first film in seven years, with the director taking credits on dramas Cry Wolf and The Crown in between. The new feature grew out of research into witch hunts in Denmark sparked by its Protestant Reformation of 1536 which resulted in more than 1,000 executions. “I thought I was going to do a film about that but as I dived into the witch hunts in Denmark, I found it difficult to relate to the perpetrators, the witch hunters. I always gravitate towards telling stories where it’s more hazy, messy and sticky,” she explains. As she and longtime writing partner Maren Louise Käehne moved away from the idea, they came across pictures of Danish women being punished in public after World War Two for their relationships with German soldiers. Women having their heads shaved and being beaten and stripped in the street for fraternizing with Germans happened across Europe in the wake of the war. “It started a discussion around the fact that both sides were wrong and both sides were right and the idea that after the war, you punish whomever you can get your hands on and whomever you can punish without being punished yourself… and that’s often the women… that was really the starting point,” says el-Toukhy. The pair then came across the work of Danish academic Annette Warring and her 1994 paper entitled “Pro-German girls – during occupation and judicial reckoning”. Warring estimated that at least 50,000 Danish women had been in relationships with German soldiers over the course of the five-year occupation, but that only a handful had been informers or supporters of Nazi Germany. Her paper noted that under Denmark’s policy of cooperation with Germany following its 1940 invasion, fraternizing with German soldiers was not unlawful, either during the occupation or under post-World War Two legislation. She suggested that the post-world war purges and humiliations had been sparked rather by sexist notions around appropriate female sexuality and morality and the belief that “woman’s sexuality was national property”. “She got a lot of heat for that at that time in the 90s, the war generation was still alive and continued to dominate the narrative on the war… we dug into her study and that was really the starting point.” El-Toukhy suggests Denmark’s tactical appeasement of Germany, because as a small nation it had little other choice, blurred the lines between cooperation and collaboration, with the resistance only really strengthening in the lead up to the end of the war. “We kept our government and our society going, but we were at the same time oppressed by the Germans… that became the whole discussion after the war,” she says. “People got punished for having collaborated, and the ‘horizontal collaborators’ would be part of that cleaning up,” she continues. “Then there would be people who were never punished because they were too vital a part of society… people with factories, doctors. It became too complicated to punish them, because then everything would come to a standstill. The women were an easy target”. The shame carried by these women after they were outed, publicly humiliated and then ostracised carried down through generations. “Their children are now around my mother’s age, 70, 80 and even the next generation live in the shadow of that story,” says el-Toukhy. Tapping into Hitchcock & Scola Protagonist Marie is not based on one single real-life character but is rather a composite drawing on all of el-Toukhy’s research. “She’s based on everyone and no-one. She’s not a specific person,” she explains. Marie’s story also grew out of el-Toukhy’s questions around what kind of societal structures allow for a woman to humiliated and physically attacked with public approval on the street. “While working with the subject matter of the female body as a battlefield, I became interested in how fellow citizens can do that to a person. What structures are in place in a society in order for that to happen, and how do these structures look at home. The story grew from there.” The idea of telling the story through the genre of a psychological thriller came with time, as el-Toukhy and Käehne grappled with how to being something new to the the World War Two setting. “It is easy to fall into the trap of making a pastiche of everything you’ve seen over the years,” she says. “I also felt people glazed over a little bit when I pitched the idea, even if I think that’s unfair because there’s so many stories we haven’t told about women so let’s tell those stories and then say we’re over and done with that period. “The idea was to make it entertaining, for lack of better words, to make it a thrill to watch even though the subject matter is quite serious. We also had the ambition of doing something that doesn’t look like a classic Second World War or post-World War Two film.” The feature follows Marie over the course of five days with “camera almost sitting on her shoulder”. “The camera is never alone with other with characters apart from these drops of zeitgeist where we dive into the energy, the chaos and the time on a more philosophical level, but the idea of always sticking to her was very much also because I had this visionthat if I were to do a World War II film or a post-World War II period drama, it should have a different flavor. I was digging to find that.” There is also a Hitchcock feel as Marie observes other inhabitants of the swanky mansion block which is the main location through the windows of other apartments, and the spectator is left asking who is watching her back. El-Toukhy also cites Ettore Scola’s 1977 period drama A Special Day ( Una giornate particolare ), starring Sophia Loren as a Rome housewife opposite Marcello Mastroianni as her neighbour who remain at home the day Adolf Hitler visits Benito Mussolini. “There were the windows there as well and a sense that everyone is watching, that constant fear that someone can see you and what do they see?… It seemed like a good symbol also of Marie’s alienation in a way… she’s part of this fancy setup, but at the same time she’s standing on the outside of it.” Woman Unknown TrustNordisk El-Toukhy also had clear ideas for aesthetics of the film, with the color red running as leitmotif throughout the film, captured in Marie’s clothing, the red of the Danish flag or swastikas daubed on the homes of suspected collaborators. “I had this idea that while I was not going to do a black and white film, I wanted it to be almost desaturated but in color, so we would only work with black, red, white. The Danish flag is red and white and of course the Nazi flag is black and white on red and then we had the greys and the browns. We ended up with this film which almost looks like it’s black and white with a splash of red,” she says. El-Toukhy sees the color scheme as a way of showing the Danish population’s efforts to reassert a sense of national identity after the war. “As a filmmaker, there are so many decisions and you spend so much time figuring out, or at least I do, on how to infuse a film with a subconscious, like that something that speaks to the audience’s subconscious,” she explains. “The color scheme is like my own interpretation, and probably the audience will never see this, but nationalism was really on the rise… We had to kind of rebuild our narrative because we were collaborating with the Germans, and of course also because of the atrocities and the complicity during the war… that idea of having these colors as almost a nationalist signature was a big inspiration and energized me during the shooting of the film.” Woman Unknown is produced by Mikael Rieks ( Land of Mine ) for Nordisk Film Production A/S in co-production with Nafta Films, Nordisk Film Production Sweden and Film i Väst. title: Jane Fonda Slams “Tech Bros, Oligarchs and Billionaires” for Wanting to Live Forever With Robots: “That’ll Be Their Babies”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 3:47am Diane Von Furstenberg and Jane Fonda pose together during an honorees lunch ahead of the DVF Awards on Sept. 3, 2026. The luncheon was held at the Venice, Italy home of von Furstenberg and Barry Diller. Diane von Furstenberg watched as Jane Fonda opened up on a range of subjects from Hollywood mergers to toxic politics on Thursday in Venice, Italy and couldn’t help but notice something about the iconic actress and activist. “You are so much stronger than you’ve ever been,” praised the fashion designer as Fonda came quickly with a reason for her steely spirit. “Well, I’m almost 90, and so it’s easier to be so. I’ve always been brave. I just didn’t always know what to be brave about until my mid-30s. It’s like resilience, you’re either born with it, or you’re not,” said Fonda, per reports in Variety, WWD and The Wrap. Related Stories General News Diane Von Furstenberg to Honor Jane Fonda in Venice; Tina Brown and Karlie Kloss to Present Critic’s Appreciation Dolly Parton, a Hollywood Treasure Who Lit Up the Screen With Her Authentic Self The discussion happened on a busy Thursday in Venice for both women as von Furstenberg mounted her 17th annual DVF Awards, an event designed to spotlight “extraordinary women” and global changemakers dedicated to making the world a better place. As such, von Furstenberg selected a roster of five honorees to fete: Fonda, Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Amor Mottley, Pulitzer Prize-winning photojournalist Lynsey Addario, Food4Education founder and CEO Wawira Njiru and author, advocate and survivor Gisèle Pelicot. Held at Teatro Carlo Goldoni, the ceremony also featured media maven Tina Brown, model and entrepreneur Karlie Kloss and Anita Hill as presenters, with a performance by singers Noa and Mira Awad. “These women are the very best of humanity,” said von Furstenberg upon taking the stage on a date that coincided with the death of feminist icon Gloria Steinem. Both von Furstenberg and Fonda dedicated the night to Steinem. “Gloria Steinem, the superwoman feminist icon and my very dear friend passed away. As we commit to continue to follow her path, I would like to dedicate this evening to her.” Said Fonda during her speech: “Tonight is dedicated to Gloria Steinem, and I do believe that she lives on in the changed lives of so many women, including my own.” She delivered remarks in front of an audience that included von Furstenberg’s significant other , billionaire Barry Diller , Huma Abedin Soros, Jewel, Edward Enninful, Cornelia Brandolini, Georgina Brandolini, Mayor of Venice Simone Venturini, Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, California Governor Gavin Newsom’s wife Jennifer Siebel Newsom, Hamilton South, Jürgen Teller, influential interior designer and art dealer Axel and May Vervoordt, Fareed Zakaria, Dries van Noten and more. Following the ceremony, guests gathered for a buffet dinner at Moro Restaurant at Palazzo Franchetti, hosted in partnership with Casa Tua, which will open a Venice location at the palazzo in early 2027. Von Furstenberg also welcomed the honorees into her home earlier in the day for a special luncheon. Also taking place during the DVF Awards event was a press gathering that saw journalists reportedly grilling Fonda on a variety of subjects that she was game to discuss. Credit that strength for how Fonda tackled the proposed Paramount Pictures merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, the fallout surrounding Mark Ruffalo’s comments against the merger amid claims of antisemitism, data centers, climate change and “tech bros, oligarchs and billionaires” attempting to live forever. Of the latter, Fonda stated, “They want to live forever, while they’re killing the rest of us. There’s two things: Most of these guys, these tech bros and these oligarchs and billionaires, they feel that the laws that the rest of us live by don’t matter to them, including the laws of physics. Natural laws. They’re going to live forever. The other [thing] is that because these guys can’t have babies, they’ll create robots. That’ll be their babies, and they’ll just turn the rest of us into tradwives, who have a lot of babies too. Then they’ll take away the vote. Can you believe it? And we’re not going to stand for it.” Fonda, who got to know Paramount boss David Ellison while making her long-running hit show Grace and Frankie for Netflix, then slammed the proposed merger but said it’s nothing personal to her friend. “They’re carrying so much debt. The Ellisons are carrying so much debt, and it’s being postponed now, so that they have to pay these huge sums. The merger would be terrible for consumers. Prices would go up. Thousands and thousands of people would lose their jobs, and as a creative, the fewer studios there are, the fewer places that we can take our products. We lose bargaining power. Unions lose their power,” said Fonda. “There’s a very robust and growing movement to stop the mergers. It’s sad for me because I like David Ellison very much. David’s Skydance financed Grace and Frankie , my 7-year-long run for Netflix. I got to know him, and I like him, but that doesn’t change things. This is not a personal thing.” She’s not scared of speaking out, nor is she afraid of the president. “I’ve had my life. [President Donald] Trump can do nothing to me. I’m not scared, but that’s not true for everyone,” she said as she then encouraged others to support the Committee for the First Amendment, which she launched. “More and more people are speaking out because their whole lives are at risk right now. AI could take everything away, and then data centers are being put in their neighborhoods, so there’s been a shift in the U.S. Things are changing. Republicans and Democrats alike are saying, ‘No, you’re not going to put a data center in my community.’ We can see now that even MAGA members are not liking the fact that their leaders are profiting off misery and cruelty. They don’t like the chaos that’s happening.” Fonda also doesn’t like how Ruffalo is being treated amid antisemitism claims for opposing the merger. “Larry Ellison, because he doesn’t like Mark Ruffalo’s position on the merger, accuses him of antisemitism, when he said nothing that isn’t within his constitutional right to say. It’s a tactic they’re using. He should be ashamed of himself, Larry Ellison. But there’s a lot of support for Mark. A lot of people came forward.” Amid so much activist work and bold statements, Fonda also said she misses her other job in front of other kinds of cameras. “After five years of not working as an actor, I have to confess, much as I love the work that I do with my comrades in the movement, I miss the process of becoming somebody else. It is such a thrilling process. I love it. I miss it,” said Fonda, who was quick to add that she’s developing an adaptation of the bestselling novel The Correspondent by Virginia Evans. “I’m doing it for Lionsgate with the film company called Hidden Pictures. We have a good first draft, and we’re looking for a director,” she teased. Von Furstenberg and the Diller-von Furstenberg Family Foundation launched the DVF Awards in 2010 as a way to spotlight and support “extraordinary women” dedicated to “transforming the lives of other women; women who have had the courage to fight, the strength to survive and the leadership to inspire.” Five trophies are handed out to women, along with a grant to each honoree, a gift bestowed to their respective nonprofit organizations to help propel and support their work. See more from inside the event below. Huma Abedin, Lynsey Addario, Karlie Kloss, Diane Von Furstenberg and Wawira Njiru at the luncheon. Said Addario: “We cannot let the horrors around us become running statistics. We must stand for freedom of the press, and for the importance of journalism as one of the fundamental principles of democracy.” A shot of the atmosphere during the DVF Awards inside Teatro Carlo Goldoni. Diane Von Furstenberg speaks during the DVF Awards in Venice, Italy on Sept. 6, 2026. Karlie Kloss, Tina Brown and Jane Fonda. Brown feted Addario by saying, “To say that Lynsey Addario is one of the world’s greatest war photographers is to understate the case. She’s one of the world’s greatest photographers, period. She makes images you could gaze at for hours — and others that are hard to look at for even a few seconds, because what they depict is so harrowing.” Courtesy of DVF Awards Tina Brown, Barry Diller and Karlie Kloss Courtesy of DVF Awards Barry Diller catches up with Jane Fonda while Diane Von Furstenberg chats with Simone Venturini. Amina Mohammed, Mia Mottley, Wawira Njiru, Karlie Kloss, Tina Brown, Lynsey Addario, Jane Fonda, Anita Hill, Gisele Pelicot and Diane Von Furstenberg Courtesy of DVF Awards Honorees Jane Fonda and Gisele Pelicot with Diane Von Furstenberg. Courtesy of DVF Awards Said Fonda in closing: “Most importantly, we have to stay hopeful. I’m hopeful because I’m giving it 100 percent. And hope is a muscle when you use it.” Courtesy of DVF Awards THR

title: Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 3:05am Tony Gatlif at the Cannes Film Festival in 2025 Kristy Sparow/Getty Images Director Tony Gatlif , who was known for films such as Gadjo Dilo exploring Roma culture, died in the Southern French town of Arles on September 3. He was 77. The director was born Michel Boualem Dahmani in Algiers on September 10, 1948, to a Kabyle father and mother of Andalusian and Gitane origin. He had a difficult childhood, growing up in poverty in slums on the outskirts of the Algerian capital, which he quit for France at age 14 in the early 1960s. After a period of precarity and petty criminality, a meeting with his idol, actor Michel Simon, opened the door to a dramatic arts course in Germain-en-Laye outside of Paris, after the latter wrote a letter of recommendation. Related Stories News Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom & Paramount International Boss Was 55 News Gloria Steinem Dies: Feminist Icon And Activist & Co-Founder Of Ms. Magazine Was 92 While gaining experience as an actor, Gatlif gradually started creating his own original work based on his own experiences and exploring the culture of his Roma origins. Watch on Deadline He broke into directing in 1975 with La tête en Ruines , followed by the Spain-shot and set drama Corre Gitano , about a young gypsy man accused of a crime he did not commit. It was the first among a series of films exploring the culture and challenges of Europe’s Roma people. In 1992, he won Cannes Un Certain Regard prize for Latcho Drom , a documentary about gypsy music. He followed this with one of this best known films, Gadjo Dilo ( The Crazy Stranger ) , starring Romain Duris as a Frenchman who travels to Romania in search of Roma singer, whose voice he has heard on tapes recorded by his late father. The film premiered at the Locarno Film Festival in 1997 where it won the Silver Leopard. Gatlif would go on to win Best Director in Cannes in 2004, with the autobiographical drama Exils , reuniting him with Duris and also featuring Lubna Azabal in the cast. title: Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 3:02am PT Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’ By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest George Clooney Says the Government Shouldn’t Regulate AI: ‘These Are Not the People You Want to Entrust the Holy Grail With’ 1 hour ago Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’ 3 hours ago ‘Jupiter’ Director Alexandre Smia on Making a Nuclear Thriller That Suddenly Feels Terrifyingly Real: ‘We’ve Entered the Third Nuclear Age’ 8 hours ago See All Getty Images Venice jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal revealed that she experimented with artificial intelligence to transform Dakota Johnson into Marilyn Monroe for her short film “Flesh Impact” which plays on the Lido. But she ended up scrapping it because she felt that it stripped Johnson’s performance of the very humanity that made it compelling. Speaking at the symposium alongside composer Alexandre Desplat, filmmakers Lee Daniels and Shannon Murphy, producer Lorenzo Mieli and artist Marc Quinn, Gyllenhaal said the short portrays a 100-year-old Marilyn Monroe with flashbacks to Marilyn Monroe when she’s in her 30s which Johnson plays. Related Stories 'One Piece' Season 3 Casts Its Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka Lee Jung-eun, Kim Moo-yul Board Netflix's Action-Noir Series 'The Shooter' “And the people who commissioned this project from me asked me to use AI. And I thought — I mean, they weren’t using OpenAI, they were using licensable AI, training it off of Marilyn Monroe films that we had licensed. And I went for it. I was like, all right, I’m curious, I don’t know, let’s see,” she says. Popular on Variety “The idea was that we trained it on her, we then put her face on Dakota’s face. We worked hard at it, and in the end, I threw it away because what was coming through Dakota playing Marilyn Monroe was so much more moving, human, alive,” she revealed during the symposium which was presented by Finch & Partners and CAA. “It fundamentally did not work. All the reasons we decided to make this project to begin with were, were, were, were killed off in the AI version,” she continued. Besides the creative shortcomings of AI, she stressed there’s also talked about the “huge environmental issues” it raises. “In America anyway, there’s a big conversation in South Memphis about the data centers. That’s a problem, so we should acknowledge that.” She also pointed that even Geoffrey Hinton, the pioneering computer scientist often referred to as the “Godfather of AI,” is “ringing bells of alarm.” “He said that he thought that we should program AI with a maternal instinct,” she said. “Because what other model is there of a less intelligent creature kind of controlling a more intelligent creature than a baby and its mother?” “I was like, first of all, so fascinating, but what does that mean to program AI with a maternal instinct coming from the godfather — that’s what he’s called — of AI?” On the financial standpoint, she said found the whole “democratization” argument that AI is supposed to provide to filmmakers unconvincing because it comes from people who are behind these AI softwares. “It concerns me a little bit because they own it. Who’s making the money off it? The people that are pitching that,” she joked, drawing an applause from the crowd. Ultimately, filmmakers and talent might lose out if AI starts being used more frequently to make commercial movies. She recalled being told that soon enough, “$40 million will now be able to cost $4 million if you do it with AI… and maybe even eventually $40,000 — which is what you were talking about in terms of democratizing or opening opportunities to people who wouldn’t otherwise have them.” “But the thing is, is if you can make a commercial good enough movie for $40,000 or even for $4 million, who’s gonna give you $10 million to do it the old way? Nobody. I mean, maybe there’s a tiny, tiny little market for that.
