title: Bendita Film Sales Snags Norma Vila’s Sitges Competition Title ‘Carapace’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 3:02am PT Bendita Film Sales Snags Norma Vila’s Sitges Competition Title ‘Carapace’ (EXCLUSIVE) Starring Nagore Aranburu ('Querer,' 'Sundays'), the psychological thriller centers on a mother gripped by uncontrollable despair when her teenage daughter decides to leave home to study By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Bendita Film Sales Snags Norma Vila’s Sitges Competition Title ‘Carapace’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago France TV Distribution’s Mystery Drama ‘Our Missing Sons’ Set for Unifrance Rendez-Vous Market Debut 1 day ago Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit ‘Congo Boy’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All 'Carapace' Courtesy of Bendita Film Sales Bendita Film Sales has acquired international rights to Norma Vila ’s psychological horror thriller “Salitre” (“Carapace”) ahead of its premiere at the Sitges Film Festival ’s Fantàstic In-Competition Selection. Vila’s debut feature stars Nagore Aranburu, star of Series Mania top laureate “Querer” and winner of this year’s supporting actress Goya Award for “Sundays,” and Haizea Carneros (“ Sacamantecas ”) as a mother and daughter whose relationship grows increasingly tense. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast In “Salitre,” when her teenage daughter Nerea decides to leave home to study, Maite is gripped by despair. For Maite, her daughter’s departure is more than a separation: it threatens to destroy the world she has built with her. Popular on Variety As Nerea prepares to leave, Maite’s fear begins to contaminate everything. Something seems to spread throughout the house, seeping into the intimacy they share and giving shape to what Maite cannot put into words. Courtesy of Bendita Film Sales Soon, Maite cuts herself off from the world and becomes obsessed with keeping her daughter at home, turning care into control and love into possession. As her obsession threatens to destroy what she loves most, Maite must confront the monster that has awakened within her: let her daughter go, or hold on to her and lose her forever. While “Carapace” may be Vila’s first feature, the director has impressed with her acclaimed previous works, winning twice the Syfy Award for best Spanish short at the San Sebastián Horror and Fantasy Film Festival: in 2016 for “Jules D.” and in 2019 for “El fin de todas las cosas.” “What drew us to ‘Carapace’ is the way Norma Vila lets the horror take hold of something painfully recognizable: a mother who cannot bear to see her daughter leave,” explained Luis Renart, head of Bendita Film Sales. “Something you can’t quite name creeps into the closeness between them and starts to spread, but the film never stops being about two people who love each other. It’s exactly the kind of genre cinema we love: singular, uncompromising, and made by a filmmaker with a voice of her own. We’re taking it to Sitges expecting genre audiences to embrace it, and we don’t think they’ll be the only ones.” A largely Basque production, “Carapace” is produced by Bilbao-based Ipuin Kontalaria and Euskadi Movie along with Pris&Batty Films, Bondi Stories and Festival Films in association with broadcasters EITB and RTVE. “We’re thrilled to partner with Bendita Film Sales, whose passion and international reach make them the ideal team to bring ‘Carapace’ to audiences worldwide,” added producer Eduardo Carneros of Euskadi Movie. “We’re especially excited to launch the film with its world premiere at Sitges and hope this will be the beginning of a strong international journey for a film we believe is both distinctive and deeply cinematic.” Shot on location in the northern region of Biskaia and neighboring Cantabria, the €2.5 million ($2.9 million) production was supported by the Basque government, the Bizkaia Tax Incentive and Comunidad de Madrid. The Sitges Film Festival runs Oct. 8-18. title: ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile’ Review: War Rages On, as Does the Journalistic Resistance, in an Essential Chronicle of Reporters Under Fire
full_text: × Skip to main content By Jordan Mintzer Plus Icon Jordan Mintzer View All September 4, 2026 2:30am 'My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile' Cinetic If part one of director Julia Loktev’s sprawling and essential 12-hour chronicle of journalism under fire concluded, like any good piece of serial storytelling, with a veritable cliffhanger, part two covers the long and painful aftermath following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By that point, we’ve come to know the handful of independent reporters — most of them women accused of being “foreign agents” by Putin’s government — whom Loktev documented during the tense months leading up to the war, showing how they held fast to their beliefs while their country began to crumble around them. Related Stories Movies 'Oasis' Director on Asking Uncomfortable Questions About Exclusion and Why Violence Is "Like a Virus" Movies 'The End of Times' Is an AI-Assisted Film Essay on Trauma That Wants to "Politicize Mental Illness" (Exclusive Venice Trailer) My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile The Bottom Line Life — and journalism — during wartime. Venue: Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition) Cast: Anna Nemzer, Valeria Ratnikova, Ksenia Mironova, Elena Kostyucheko, Yana Kuchina, Irina Dolinina, Alesya Marokhovskaya, Peter Ruzavin, Nataliya Gumenyuk, Sonya Groysman Director, cinematographer: Julia Loktev 5 hours 56 minutes In the second half of this epic study of persecution and resistance, we watch these courageous, resourceful young journos deal with forced exile, scattering across several countries and continents as the Russian state continues to pursue them for bogus offenses like spreading “fake news.” Given what they already dealt with back home, it’s no surprise they exhibit a fair amount of sangfroid and journalistic integrity as they wheel their carry-on luggage from one airport or Airbnb to another, trying to find a place to live and especially to work, which they continue to do while the conflict rages on. Such persistence doesn’t, however, shield them from a deep sense of loss, loneliness, anxiety and especially guilt as the citizens of an oppressive, war-crime-committing superpower, even if they’re also being oppressed themselves. One of them sums up that sentiment early on by quoting a friend, who quips: “It’s like 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew.” That Kafkaesque sense of never being fully safe, of never being at peace with oneself, hovers over much of My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile, though it also never stops these women from getting the truth out. Divided into five chapters that stretch from the invasion until the spring of 2026, the doc stays glued to its reporters through thick and thin — clearly a logistical feat given how they constantly change locations after visas are granted or denied, newsrooms opened or shuttered, and the world as they once knew it is transformed into a continual state of precarity. “It’s like my life is totally in someone else’s hands,” comments Valeria Ratnikova, aka Lera, who’s only 23 when we first see her in a taxi in Istanbul alongside Ksenia Mironova, aka Ksysusha. (The loving Russian diminutives all the characters give each other underscore their sense of solidarity.) Lera’s trajectory, which takes her from Russia to Turkey to Latvia and finally to the Netherlands, serves as something of a throughline in an ensemble piece that has nearly a dozen protagonists. As the youngest anchorwoman at the independent news station TV Rain, which shuts down in Moscow as soon as the war breaks out, Lera finds herself on the run along with her hardworking colleagues, all of whom are forced to pack their bags (or more like one bag) and rush to the airport before Putin tosses them in jail. Trying to find their footing abroad while reporting on what’s happening in Ukraine, including the many atrocities committed in the early months of the conflict, the TV Rain team faces untold challenges to get the news out. Not only do they continue to be persecuted from afar — Lera will be convicted in absentia to seven and a half years in prison for working for an “undesirable organization” — but the channel nearly folds when a newscaster uses the term “our army” when referring to the war crimes committed by the Russian military, causing a scandal in their host country of Latvia and, eventually, the suspension of their broadcasting license. The catch-22 situation the reporters all find themselves in — either stay in Russia and face prison, or flee abroad and face both personal exile and anti-Russian prejudice — is something they accept as par for the course, well aware that those dying in Ukraine do not have the luxury of that option. “Like it or not, the war is being waged in our name too,” one of them comments, taking responsibility as both a Russian citizen and an independent journalist who refuses to bow down to the Kremlin’s demands. title: ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 2:30am PT ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run Julia Loktev continues to wield her iPhone like a personal diary while following journalists targeted by the Kremlin. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory 2 days ago ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher 4 days ago ‘Mustache’ Review: A Delightfully Anxious Pakistani American Coming-of-Age Comedy 4 weeks ago See All Venice Film Festival Following her mammoth five-hour odyssey “ My Undesirable Friends: Part I — Last Air in Moscow ,” Julia Loktev ’s sequel remains just as riveting, if not more so, in its continued depiction of journalists escaping the Russian government. Its predecessor’s endpoint (one Loktev could not have foreseen when she began shooting on her iPhone X) was the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and the overnight escape of her close friends from Moscow after they were branded foreign agents for reporting on war crimes. “My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile” follows their stories amidst this exodus, a globetrotting journey that proves harrowing in unexpected ways over an engrossing five chapters, spanning 355 minutes. Related Stories Netflix’s Latest Marketing Mash-Up Pairs Stella Artois With 'The Gentlemen' Netflix Orders 'Manifest' Spinoff 'Arrivals,' With a New Mystery and Cast — Announced on 8/28, Of Course That figure might seem imposing to the uninitiated, but Loktev and co-editor Michael Taylor have, once again, crafted a conversational epic that imbues each twist and turn with enormous stakes. It’s hard not to get invested in the lives of Part I’s subjects and Part II’s newcomers alike. Speaking truth to power with the online tools at their disposal, this murderer’s row consists of lively, awkward, driven, beautiful, lovestruck and above-all complicated people, all caught in impossible personal and professional deadlocks and weighed down by immigrant uncertainty. Popular on Variety “Exile” begins with a brisk, five-minute recap of events, which goes a long way toward reintroducing Loktev’s subjects. It also imbues the film with immediate tension. With only small suitcases and the clothes on their backs, the young journalists of independent outfits like TV RAIN find themselves suddenly scattered across cities like Warsaw, Istanbul, Prague and Tel Aviv. They go anywhere that will grant them temporary refuge, even as they wrestle with their own ethics in relation to each new nation’s politics, when compared and contrasted with their homeland. This sets the stage for a film in which firmly held beliefs are placed under microscopes — by the subjects themselves, and by critics on either side of the Ukraine/Russia divide. As some reporters begin broadcasting from Latvia, a sense of temporariness pervades each interaction, no matter how casual. Authors, reporters and podcasters alike are forced to consider the impact of their words, and their own potential complicity in their country’s actions, as stepping even a toe out of line might result in further expulsion. When speaking truth to power, nothing is a given. Unlike the mere six months covered by the first film, the sequel spans several years and covers major events, from continuing Russian aggression to the killing of opposition leader Alexei Navalny. Loktev’s scattered cast ends up experiencing these global shockwaves firsthand, reporting on everything from political poisonings to mass civilian graves — in person if they can, or remotely, with the help of anonymous sources. Some move or return to Kyiv. Others make their way further west, like to the United States, where they observe an uncanny authoritarianism taking hold. The film’s chilling tapestry is interwoven with its subjects’ gallows humor. As their challenges mount, sometimes all they can do is laugh at the absurdity, though at least they’re laughing together. However, enough time is spent with them as individuals that their bleak loneliness starts to bleed through the screen. Twentysomething Ksenia Mironova finds ways to move forward in her career, though her fiancé remains a state prisoner. The older Anna Nemzer (the film’s co-director) grows more frayed, as each emigration means having to uproot her adolescent daughter. TV RAIN anchors like Valeria Ratnikova face both scrutiny and legal threats, while for those still reporting from (or escaping) Ukrainian war zones, the dangers are more pressing. Even as they move between borders, bullseyes remain painted on their backs — though they each maintain that the people whose stories they tell have it infinitely worse. One has to wonder if Loktev feels the same about her subjects. A one-woman team who remains mostly unseen, she finds herself hopping between cities for years on end, similarly sacrificing peace of mind to bring vital narratives to light. Whether or not she could have hired an additional crew or second unit, the effect of her solo flight is an emotional proximity to her subjects, who trust her enough to let their guard down in front of her smartphone. Her camera app seems to run day and night, but she and Taylor make judicious selections. While Part I felt more straightforward in its unfurling, Part II appears to condense time even more deftly, jump-cutting within and between exchanges without ever losing momentum or conversational clarity. Loktev and her undesirable friends ought not to be boxed in — their work is too expansive and important. But there’s also a noticeably feminine intimacy to several scenes here, whether the subjects discuss clothing as they wrap up their lives yet again, or present themselves casually, freely and without artifice, as though the camera were merely recording for a private Instagram, or absent altogether. The film is born from journalistic ideology, but most of its subjects are women, and it takes aesthetic shape through the lens of female friendship and professional community, fanning outward from this personal place until it shades the political with remarkably familiar hues. As the sands shift beneath their feet, the subjects are practically the only constant in each other’s lives — as is Loktev, who’s there to capture them at their best and worst. Rare are the films that remain so transfixed by the conundrums inherent to living in a murky world, or that pursue the emotional and psychological dimensions of political journalism with such disarming simplicity. Let it be a warning of things to come, or a comfort once they inevitably do. There’s no untangling the two anymore. Not for people who’ve dedicated their lives to sounding the alarm, even as they wonder if they might be too late. ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Review: An Enormous, Riveting Documentary Sequel Following Reporters on the Run Reviewed online, Sept. 1, 2026. title: Jack Huston On The Tough Questions About Sexual Abuse Posed By Paul Schrader’s Film ‘The Basics Of Philosophy’: “It’s Almost Become A Taboo Subject” – Venice Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Bucking Fastard’ Review: Werner Herzog’s Eccentric Comedy Is A Bittersweet Tale Of Unrequited Lovers – Venice Film Festival ‘The Girl With The Leica’ Review: Love Is War In Alina Marazzi’s Unconventional Biopic Of A Pioneering War Photographer – Venice Film Festival View All September 4, 2026 2:03am ‘The Basics Of Philosophy’ Paul Schrader writes great parts for great actors, and has been doing so for 50 years, since Robert De Niro played Travis Bickle in Martin Scorsese ’s Taxi Driver . Since then, to name but a few, he’s given us William Devane in Rolling Thunder , Richard Gere in American Gigolo , Willem Dafoe in Light Sleeper , Nick Nolte in Affliction and Ethan Hawke in First Reformed . Way before toxic masculinity was ever diagnosed, Schrader was rooting around in the psyches of men who, for one reason or another, just didn’t feel safe in their own skin anymore. We can now add to that list The Basics of Philosophy , a tight, literate psychological drama that clocks in at a highly economical 94 minutes and yet somehow tackles one of the greatest existential questions of all time: Is it really possible to escape the past? In The Card Counter , we saw a war criminal trying to distance himself from his involvement in the atrocities of Abu Ghraib, and in Master Gardener we met a Nazi-tattooed former white supremacist trying to start a new life in a witness protection scheme. Related Stories News Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc 'Be Brave': "We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us" - Venice Festivals George Clooney Reveals The Rule He Tries To Live By, The Uncertain Path To Acting Success & His Next Movie -- Venice Masterclass The Basics of Philosophy , however, might be the most perfect distillation of his themes so far. The great actor this time is Jack Huston , who plays philosopher lecturer John Jorrison. Jorrisen is the picture of professionalism, and an honest teacher too, as we find when he refuses to go easy on a student’s grades to stop her from failing. In a desperate last-ditch bid for clemency, the student threatens to blackmail him. It turns out to be a bluff, but there is a skeleton in his closet: As a younger man, during his post-student career as a music teacher, Jorrisen molested a teenage student called Miguel (Daniel Zovatto), a transgression covered up by his rich and therefore powerful father ( Bill Pullman ). Watch on Deadline The p-word — pedophilia — is never really mentioned, since Jorrisen is not what you might call a pedophile, having a bizarre arm’s-length courtship with an increasingly frustrated psychology professor Rebecca Richards ( Sofia Boutella ). Nevertheless, the false accusation starts him thinking about the past, the enormity of his crime (singular) and its impact on his victim. On the day of the film’s world premiere in Venice , Huston spoke to Deadline about the film’s uncompromising themes of guilt and redemption. DEADLINE: How did you get involved with this film? JACK HUSTON: I’ve known Paul on and off — God, I want to say going all the way back. He actually wanted me to be in a film called The Canyons (2013) many, many years ago. Which I didn’t do, but we’ve sort of remained friendly, and I’m very close with the producer, Braxton Pope. We worked together many, many years ago on a film called Shrink (2009). So, we’ve always had it in our minds that we’d like to work together. But when I was away working and I got a call from Braxton saying, “Listen, there’s a script that Paul wants me to read,” and he didn’t say much more than that — a bit like you watching the film, probably. You can’t really preface it with anything. He was like, “You just have to read it.” And after reading it, I thought it was first and foremost one of the best scripts I’ve read. I think it’s superb. I mean, it’s masterful. It’s Schrader through and through. He’s a bucket-list director that I’ve been dying to work with for many years. But it was only after reading the script about seven times that I finally decided to meet with Schrader and actually have a chat about it, because I really had to read it a lot to digest it. DEADLINE: Did you have any doubts? You said you read it seven times. HUSTON: Absolutely. It’s interesting; the things that scare you the most are sometimes the things that challenge you the most. I actually have a story about this. I was on set with a lovely actor called Jake Lacy, and Jake asked me, “What’s a role you’d never play?” I said I’d never play a predator, anything to do with children. It was about two months before I got Schrader’s script. And I’d also said around that time that I really wanted to work with a certain caliber of director. I was getting to a point in my life where leaving my children, leaving my wife, leaving home gets harder and harder, so you really want to be working with great people. So of course, the gods answered my question by sending me Schrader’s script, which I thought was very appropriate for where I was in my head space. OK, so it was a very difficult read, but I found it an incredibly important read. This is something me and my wife have to deal with on a daily basis. We talk about this. We have a 10-year-old and a 13-year-old. I think what Schrader does better than anybody is he tells the story of the everyman —the last suspect, almost, the person hiding in plain sight. Because that’s the truth of it. It exists everywhere in the world and it’s not usually the man who comes at you with his hands raised and a dagger in his hand. It’s usually the last person you’d ever suspect, the friendly guy, the affable man, the teacher. When I was at school, I remember my music teacher got kicked out for inappropriate behavior with a 13-year-old. So, I grew up seeing this. I mean, there’s multiple cases of teachers or music teachers having inappropriate behavior with students. And it’s about that sort of age — 13, 14, 15 — where it’s a real problem. So, I feel there’s real duty to telling this story, and I think Schrader does it so brilliantly well. DEADLINE: On top of that, you also have to be a philosophy professor. How did you approach that aspect of the role? HUSTON: Oh man, I’ve never worked harder. I read everything. I mean, it was kind of a gift and a curse, because you don’t ever want to take anything lightly. There’s not a single scene in this film that I didn’t spend months going over. Quite rightly so. I wanted to be as thoughtful approaching this role as I possibly could. It was a very, very difficult place to live in for the time I was doing it. But, as an actor, you have to put in the work. And for a film like, this and for a role like this, there is a certain amount of duty you have. I had to humanize the character first, so that we make him more relatable. And actually, by doing that, it poses the greater question, which is, can you trust anybody? And also, Spinoza’s great question, are we capable of change? Which is, I think, not for me to answer, it’s for me to pose and for audience to answer or at least debate and talk about. DEADLINE: How did you discuss this with Paul? I mean, how could you discuss your approach to the role when you were going for such ambiguity? If that makes sense. HUSTON: Yes, it does make sense. Paul is very matter of fact. He won’t tell you what he thinks, a lot of the time. That’s my job. And then it’s my job to not necessarily tell an audience what I think, but to perform it in a way that does leave it open-ended but allows them to make up their own minds. Perhaps the most important thing that Paul said to me on our very first Zoom was that he believes that the final act of any film, especially his films, happens when the audience leaves the cinema. It’s the conversation that ensues. So, I can tell you this much — this film is going to cause a conversation, so he’s going to succeed. Boy, is he ever. I think it’s very important that this conversation is had, though. It’s almost become a taboo subject, but it shouldn’t be. This should be pulled out from under the carpet and slammed on top of the table. This is a subject everybody should be talking, about because it’s so prevalent in society. And I spoke to multiple friends — gay, straight, I mean my wife even — and lot of them had their first sexual experiences when they were teenagers with older people. Like, people who were much older than them. And whether or not they thought they were abused, they were abused. It’s a form of abuse because it’s an older person using their stature. If it were a teacher, someone that one would mentor or look up to, it’s using that status and manipulating that and using it for their benefits. In the film, John is a much younger man when this happens. But let’s not get this wrong, it’s abuse. That’s what it is. We can’t sugarcoat that. That’s definitely abuse. But John has then spent his life after the incident in the sort of cynical way, ridding himself of any delights or pleasures to live a very straight life, to live a very plain life, no alcohol, no relationships. I think he knows what he’s done. And — with regard to the Spinoza question, which is, are we capable of change — I think that’s probably what keeps him awake at night, that exact question, because he desperately wants to change. He hopes he can. If he can’t, then he’s a monster. DEADLINE: It’s important that it’s just the one incident. I mean, 20, 30 years ago, people would just say, “Well, it only happened once,” and then they’d move on. And I think it’s very interesting that, as you say, this is still keeping him awake at night. HUSTON: I don’t think I would’ve taken this role if he was out there just abusing people. I think it’s a far more interesting and thoughtful and considered film — and performance —because of it being a single incident, because a single incident can ruin your life. A single incident can keep you awake at night. A single incident can haunt you. It doesn’t make it any better that it was once. It’s still awful. And I think that’s what I found very interesting about the character of John Jorrisen is he’s a philosophy professor. He thinks for a living. It’s his curse; he has to philosophize and think every single day. And actually, his studies have been as much about his life as those around him. I think he’s trying to be a better man, but he also takes up the idea that if we cannot live good and we will live badly. DEADLINE: It’s interesting that the film starts with an accusation — the student who says, “I know what you’ve done, I know about you.” Immediately, all the scenarios that you’ve mentioned go through the viewer’s mind. HUSTON: It’s so smart, that. I love that you brought that up because it’s like I think most people have done something bad in life. You just have to say to someone, “I know what you’ve done,” and that person will instantly go to that one thing that haunts them. “Oh my gosh, they know!” It was a very brilliant tactic. DEADLINE: It’s the perfect subject for a Paul Schrader movie, because his films are so much about tortured men looking for redemption. But who can forgive you — who has the power to forgive you — for an incident like this? HUSTON: It’s interesting, because it’s between him and Miguel, isn’t it, at the end of it? I think that’s, in John’s mind, the only person, there’s no one else to forgive him. The only person who could probably or possibly forgive him is the person he abused. He certainly can’t forgive himself. I think he’s always had it in the back of his head that it would come to this. It’s almost like a crusade, isn’t it? I think it was fascinating because Schrader writes in such a way that even in the lightest scenes, there feels like a weight. And I remember feeling this weight, and it became internal. It was in my stomach and it gnawed away at me. With everything you do, every scene you’re in, there’s something there — there’s baggage, and it feels like it’s pulling you down. You feel like you’re drowning. And I think John Jorrisen feels like he’s drowning. Even in the best moments, he feels like he’s drowning. And that’s from the choices he’s made, and that’s who he is as a man. DEADLINE: Paul’s been in a bit of a groove with these kinds of men-in-crisis movies lately, since First Reformed (2017). Did you go back and watch them again, or is that not helpful as an actor to watch? HUSTON: No, I did. I watched everything, going all the way back to Taxi Driver . I mean, it’s amazing how long he’s been playing out the man in the room with the checkered past. I think no one writes like him. And I mean this as a great compliment: He feels very European to me, because the films he makes, we don’t actually see too much in America these days, but maybe there’s a certain European flair. That’s why maybe Venice is the best place for the premiere of a film like this, because he’s posing very large and difficult questions to an audience, but they’re important questions. And I think the minute we try to censor ourselves and say we shouldn’t make films like this is the minute we censor art itself, and art should be the one place where you ask the difficult questions. And they’re not for us to answer, they’re for us to pose. Hopefully a film like this opens that conversation up and makes us much more free to talk about. And actually, when I was doing my research — which I did so much for something like this because I’d never do it without — it just really did show me that this happens daily, multiple times a day. And I think people need to be far more aware of just how dangerous the world is. And a lot of the time the abused don’t even know they’ve been abused. And I found that fascinating that it’s actually, but that doesn’t make it not abuse. That’s the point I want to get across here very much. It’s like whatever the case, however you are, even if you saw it as your sexual revolution, you were 14 and you met someone older. Like I said, my wife was dating a man when she was 16 who she thought was 18 years old. Turned out he was 29. So, every person I spoke to had some form of story or they had a story about someone else. I was like, “Wow, it really is everywhere.” So, I’m glad that someone like Paul Schrader’s around and can write something like this. DEADLINE: It’s also interesting that actors like Richard Gere and Bill Pullman are willing to take part, because those names help to sell a difficult subject matter, surely… HUSTON: Yeah, I mean they all come out for Paul because he’s brilliant and he’s a singular voice in our industry. He’s his own being, and everybody supports him. I saw Marty [Scorsese] the other day. He’s come on board as an EP and he just loves the film. He thought the film was miraculous. And I think that says a lot, because Marty’s an incredibly thoughtful filmmaker, one of the most brilliant filmmakers as we all know, but he’s somebody who understands just how important someone like Paul Schrader is and how important that voice is. And that’s ultimately why I did the film, because sometimes the things that scare you the most are the things that we have to tackle head on. I believe we made quite a brilliant film, and I’m incredibly proud of the performance. I think it’s one of the best ones I’ve ever had the opportunity to do, and it’s incredibly considered. I hope people are able to see that. DEADLINE: Guilt and remorse were a big part of the film that you directed, Day of the Fight (2023), the idea of the weight of one’s “sins”, the missed opportunities or things done wrong. It seems to me that you’re attracted to that as an element of storytelling. HUSTON: Very much. It’s so interesting you brought that up, because there’s a whole scene in Day of the Fight, where Mikey (Michael Pitt) has a conversation with his friend Patrick (John Magaro) in church. He says, “I’ve changed. I know that, but people… all they remember is the past. I’ll always be who I was, not who I am.” Which means, it doesn’t matter [that he’s changed]. He hasn’t had a drink in nine years and he doesn’t want one. But no matter what, people will always see him for who he was, not for who he is. And I think it’s a very interesting way of looking at this script, because it was when I was really philosophizing about the idea of change and redemption, and if we are able to change. And that’s why Schrader is such a sort of genius, man. He comes along and poses the question in such a brutally honest and devastating way that a lot of things I thought I knew I didn’t know, and it made me just go back to the books and just work and work and work. DEADLINE: Are you planning to direct again? What’s your next move? HUSTON: Yes, I am. I’m meant to be starting pre-production next week, but we’ll see if that bloody happens. Independent cinema at its finest! [Laughs.] We’re very, very close. My next film’s about Joseph Merrick, who was known as “The Elephant Man”, but we use the last month of his life and his childhood from 5 years old to 15, when he left home. It’s a script that I’ve written and I feel very proud to be making it later this year. The title Joseph Merrick right now, which I’m sure is subject to change. We’ll see what it’s called at the end. DEADLINE: And what attracted you to that story? HUSTON: Funny enough, my mentor was really John Hurt. I was very close with John and spent a lot of time with him and his wife — well, widow now — Anwyn. I got to live with them when they were in California and spent a lot of time with John. I will never forget that performance in that film, David Lynch’s film, and what it did to me, so there wasn’t a piece of me that wanted to make that film again, because it’s been done absolutely perfectly and brilliantly and I would never even dare. But what I did find out after a lot of reading was that there were parts of Joseph’s life that we didn’t know about. So, it’s been a beautiful exploration of this stunning figure who, against all the odds, led with kindness and generosity and beauty. And I think the world needs these stories. They need someone to look up to. And when you look at somebody who had such a horrible start in life and the afflictions that he was born with, and yet he was still able to hold himself the way he did… I think it’s a good example for people, and it’s a film I want my kids to watch. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

title: Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 1:53am PT Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Manisha Koirala Attached to Star in ‘Cowgirls & Indians,’ Set for November Texas Shoot (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Busan Market Unveils Doc Square, Launches Impact Asia as Yim Siwan Named Festival Closing Ceremony Host 4 hours ago Tamar AI’s TapNow Brings AI-Native Filmmaking to Venice Production Bridge With HappyHorse-Backed 10,000 Parallel Universes Films, Unveils Streamer Glanze 4 hours ago See All ACFM The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the market of the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), will present Doc Square 2026 from Oct. 10-13, bringing together eight partner organizations from five countries to connect Asian documentary creators with industry professionals. Launched last year, the program introduces documentary projects still in production across Asia and offers guidance on production support and distribution strategy. Related Stories Roald Dahl Drama Series Set at Netflix Starring Nicola Coughlan, Naomi Scott, Dominic West, Imelda Staunton and More Netflix Pushes Back on Tyra Banks 'Reality Check' Defamation Suit Doc Square’s centerpiece, the Documentary WIP Showcase, runs through the Asian Cinema Fund’s Asian Network of Documentary (AND) Fund alongside partner organizations from Korea, Japan, Taiwan, Indonesia and the Philippines. Newstapa Foundation and Japan’s J-Docs Hub join as new partners this year, alongside returning partners Taiwan Docs, the Taiwan Creative Content Agency, the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute, Docs by the Sea and the Film Development Council of the Philippines. Sixteen works-in-progress documentaries will pitch to festival programmers, sales companies and distributors on Oct. 10 and 11, building networks toward completion and eventual release. Popular on Variety Two new prizes debut alongside the showcase. The Impact Asia Award will go to three projects, each receiving $5,000, while the Newstapa Award gives one project KRW10 million ($7,400) along with a chance for a 60-minute cut to stream on Newstapa Foundation’s website and YouTube channel. Winners will be named at the ACFM Awards Ceremony on Oct. 13. Doc Square will also host Asia’s first Impact Day, a one-day program built around a question: what actually happens to a society after a documentary screens? Case studies from Korea, Taiwan and Japan will be compiled into an 80-page report available at the venue. The Korea study draws on roughly 2,800 works released between 1988 and 2025, alongside a survey of 88 creators and interviews with 19 industry professionals. The Taiwan study traces how “Small Talk” moved from theatrical release into education and public screening use, while the Japan study looks at how “What Should We Have Done?,” a documentary with unusually strong box-office results, built audience relationships through mini-theaters, festivals and independent screenings. Additional Doc Square sessions cover co-production, festival strategy and funding. The Documentary Festival & Fund Talk on Oct. 10 brings together festival programmers and funders from around the world, while the Current State of Documentary Co-Production splits into an Asia-focused session on Oct. 10 and a Korea-focused session on Oct. 11. On the program’s final day, “AND Talk & Share” gives this year’s AND Fund recipients a private workshop to discuss the challenges of finishing their projects. Elsewhere at the festival, actor Yim Siwan has been named sole host of the 31st BIFF closing ceremony, where the festival will present its Busan Awards, introduced last year to honor Competition winners. Yim debuted in 2012 with the series “Moon Embracing the Sun” and moved into film the following year with “The Attorney,” a role that pushed back against typecasting for idol-turned-actors. He built his reputation further as office worker Jang Geu-rae in “Misaeng” (2014), and later credits include “The Merciless” (2017), “Run On” (2020), “Boyhood” (2023) and “Unlocked” (2023). He joined “Squid Game” for Season 2 and Season 3, and appeared in the 2025 film “Mantis.” His honors include the Popularity Award at the 2014 Blue Dragon Film Awards, Best New Actor (TV) at the 2015 Baeksang Arts Awards, Best Supporting Actor at the 2022 Buil Film Awards, and Best Actor at the 2024 Blue Dragon Series Awards. The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15, at the Busan Cinema Center and throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13. title: Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 4, 2026 1:43am PT Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Propel U.K. Box Office to Best August Since 2018 2 hours ago Magdalena Koleśnik and Kay Greidanus to Lead Finn Szumlas’ Debut Feature ‘Stairway to Earth’ as Production Starts (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago ‘Smile’ Producers Temple Hill and Anton Team With YouTube Horror Star Sam Evenson for ‘Ignore It,’ Lily Collias to Lead Feature Adaptation of Viral Short (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All Credit: Alicja Kozak, Teska Overbeeke Dutch filmmaker Finn Szumlas has started principal photography on his debut feature “Stairway to Earth,” kicking off a 5-week shoot in the Netherlands. Leading the film is Polish star Magdalena Koleśnik (“Sweat”) and Dutch actor Kay Greidanus (“Dit Zijn Wij”), playing two strangers who meet up after a one night stand at at a summer music festival and have one day to make the biggest decision of their lives. Related Stories YouTube Creator Kevin Langue Is Bringing His Comedy Channels to Netflix Lee Jung-eun, Kim Moo-yul Board Netflix's Action-Noir Series 'The Shooter' The script for “Stairway to Earth” iwas written by Szumlas and Olga Ponjee. Producers include Edwin Goldman for Goldman Film and Petra Goedings for Phanta Film, with Polish co-producer Ewa Puszczyńska bringing her experience having produced numerous award-winning films including “Cold War,” “Ida” and “The Zone of Interest.” Dutch public broadcaster NTR is also a co-production partner. Popular on Variety Set in present day Leiden, Netherlands and inspired by by the real-life story of how director Finn Szumlas’ Polish father and Danish mother met and became a family, “Stairway to Earth” is described as an “emotional, intimate portrait of chance, choice, and the lives that are shaped by both.” The film follows Jan and Luiza, who share a single night at a summer music festival in Poland — an impulsive moment of passion that was never intended to last. Weeks later, they awkwardly reunite at a clinic in the Netherlands where Luiza has made an appointment to terminate the unexpected pregnancy. With twenty-four hours until the procedure, they walk through the historic streets of Leiden during the city’s annual Leidens Ontzet celebrations. Wandering through a city alive with music, history, and celebration, two people with very different lives begin to imagine a future neither of them expected. Luiza, an ambitious Polish professional preparing to leave for New York. Jan, a Dutch gardener happy to let life unfold one day at a time. Between them lies a single day that could change everything. “’Stairway to Earth’ is a deeply personal project for me, inspired as it is by how my own parents met. We have relocated the story to contemporary times, and I am super excited to be shooting in the very streets where I grew up,” said Szumlas. “As soon as I saw Magdalena and Kay together, I knew that I had found the intimacy, courage and chemistry I was looking for, and that the film was going to work. The backdrop of Leidens Ontzet will almost be a character in the film too, and we will capture the life, music and the rawness of the street festivities on Super 16mm.” The film production team includes Katja van den Broeke (cinematographer), Jorien Sont (production designer), Manon Blom (costume designer), Pur Thijs (hair and make-up designer), Saida van der Reijd (casting director), Saskia Kievits (editor), and Vincent Sinceretti (sound design). “Stairway to Earth” is supported by the Netherlands Film Fund, Polish Film Institute, NTR, CoBo, and Creative Europe MEDIA. title: Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Competition Filmmaker May El-Toukhy On Gender Imbalance: “I’ve Been The Only Woman In Many, Many Settings” Tony Gatlif Dies: ‘Gadjo Dilo’ Director Whose Work Celebrated Roma Culture Was 77 Lorenzo Mieli Talks Grappling With AI For Diesel Founder Renzo Rosso Bio-Doc ‘Be Brave’: “We Need To Master It, Rather Than Let AI Master Us” – Venice View All September 4, 2026 1:27am Mario Gianani and Lorenzo Mieli at the premiere for Nessun Dolore at the Venice Film Festival, September 3, 2026 Getty Images Italian producer Lorenzo Mieli is one of the speakers at the CAA and Finch & Partners The Future of… Creativity forum unfolding today on the fringes of the Venice Film Festival. The symposium at the La Scuola Grande di Santa Maria della Misericordia, also featuring George Clooney, Venice Artistic Director Alberto Barbera and jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal as guest speakers, will explore the future of storytelling in the age of AI . Venice regular Mieli is well placed to make a meaningful contribution to the discussion as the producer of Be Brave , the first ever documentary made with AI to screen in Venice’s official selection. Related Stories Festivals George Clooney Reveals The Rule He Tries To Live By, The Uncertain Path To Acting Success & His Next Movie -- Venice Masterclass Festivals 'Wild Horse Nine' Gets Rapturous 14-Minute Standing Ovation At Venice World Premiere The film appears to be a classic bio-doc in which director Francesco Carrozzini attempts to pin down Renzo Rosso for a portrait of his audacious career as the founder of the Diesel brand and the OTB Group – Only The Brave fashion empire, which also includes the Jil Sander, Maison Margiela, Marni and Viktor&Rolf labels. But all is not what it seems. Interviews with the likes of former Vogue Editor-in-Chief Anna Wintour; fashion designers John Galliano, Johan Lindeberg and Glenn Martens; communications guru Maurizio Marchiori, and Adriano Goldschmied, the so-called “Godfather of denim” and Rosso’s first partner on Diesel, among others, are real, even if the backdrops have sometimes been retouched. But Rosso’s interventions across the documentary are generated purely by AI as is most the “archive” material showing snapshots of his childhood, youth and early career achievements. Carrozzini, whose pursuit to track down Rosso for a face-to-face interview is interwoven into the storyline, is also AI-generated even though he exists in real life. Mieli spearheaded the project, with Mario Gianani , his partner at joint Rome-Based production house Our Films , and its COO, Gabriele Immirzi, also on board as producers. The producer’s embrace of AI may seem surprising given his past work at the forefront of human creativity, with his more than 100 credits including Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Paolo Sorrentino’s The Hand of God , Luca Guadagnino’s Queer and Sofia Coppola’s Priscilla to name but a few. But it is very much in keeping with Mieli’s pioneering track-record across his career, overseeing the growth of the The X-Factor format in Italy in the 2010s as the CEO of Fremantle Italia, or helping to usher in the Italian high-end drama boom with the groundbreaking 2015 HBO deal for Paolo Sorrentino’s The Young Pope , which led to partnerships on Saverio Costanzo’s My Brilliant Friend and Guadagnino’s We Are Who We Are . Be Brave is one of two documentaries being launched on the festival circuit by Our Films this fall alongside t he late Eleanor Coppola’s Making Marie Antoinette , which has just been announced for Telluride and then heads to the New York Film Festival. Watch on Deadline Be Brave Our Films Mieli and Gianani are also at the festival as producers on Gianni Amelio’s Out of Competition title Nessun Dolore about a Rome bookseller who finds himself on the wrong side of the law after he welcomes undocumented migrants into his home. Talking to Deadline, ahead of the Be Brave premiere Out of Competition in Venice next week, Mieli says Our Films’ exploration of AI is a natural progression. “Directors and their artistic vision are at the heart of what we do,” says Mieli. “They are the reason we keep doing this incredibly challenging job: supporting and working with directors we love, discovering new ones to love, and creating films, TV series, and documentaries, all the while striving to make something beautiful and fresh, and setting a new challenge for ourselves in the process.” “That’s the first point, and I want to frame it right away by saying we didn’t just ‘choose’ AI; rather, Francesco Carrozzini, the documentary’s director, and I decided to work with AI and challenge ourselves to truly understand what it is, to grasp the nature of this tool everyone is talking about. A tool that is so divisive, so fascinating, yet also so frightening.” Mieli adds that the decision to work with AI for the documentary also stemmed from the fact that there was very little archive material capturing Rosso’s life and career behind the scenes. Another consideration was that other companies and directors were pitching Rosso with documentary ideas and time was of the essence. “There was a lack of material that felt truly significant, authentic, vital, or compelling, beyond the usual official footage,” says Mieli. “We reviewed what was already out there and found the existing material to be very cold, mostly official interviews and promotional content. “Then, looking at the AI ​​developments emerging at the time, it struck us that AI might be the tool to recreate ‘real’ material, capturing the genuine truths we wanted to convey, while simultaneously being entirely artificial and fabricated, created using this new technology to tell the story.” Beyond the practical reasons, Mieli and Carrozzini felt the experimentation with AI as a filmmaking tool would also chime with “the two main pillars” of Rosso’s career. “Renzo Rosso has always focused on two main areas: creative freedom and innovation, he is always experimenting with new things and has a constant eye on the future; in fact, he has an obsession with the future,” says Mieli. “Everyone who has even interviewed him describes how he constantly challenges you, pushes you to look beyond what you already know, what you see, and the status quo; he urges you to imagine how people will dress tomorrow and to envision things you have never seen before.” While the decision to put AI at the heart of the documentary’s production made sense on a practical and philosophical level, Mieli recounts it was easier said than done. “The technological tool we used became both the form and the content of the documentary. That’s what led us to build the fictional narrative woven into the documentary, to show how it aligns with Renzo’s challenge of ‘Don’t be afraid’. And this was despite the fact that, when we started working on it, we didn’t really know AI; we didn’t know what we could or couldn’t achieve, how it would progress, what the risks were, or what worked and what didn’t,” he says. “Ultimately, we found ourselves grappling with AI, because it’s a tool that offers incredible possibilities but also has significant downsides, things that don’t work, aren’t interesting, or are limiting.” Our Films spent more than a year and a half developing its own AI model that would enable Carrozzini to make his film. “We worked hard and created our own model—essentially a proprietary system built on our own extensive libraries and assets that we fully owned: Francesco’s images, his photos, and videos of him speaking,” says Mieli. Mieli and Carrozzini were joined on the project by writers Michele Abatantuono and Lara Prando, and AI creative director Roberto Beragnoli, Senior Creative Producer Marco Pianigiani and Director of Photography Matteo Vieille. Editing was by Rocco Bernini and Nicole Pagin, with music by Ralf Hildenbeutel. Beragnoli oversaw the development of the tailored AI model, working with Italian company Blackstone, which has a track record in visual effects and applying AI systems to audiovisual production, while Pianigiani is credited with shaping the film’s narrative architecture and rhythm, in collaboration with the writers, AI artists and editorial team. According to detailed production notes, the model drew on established feature-film VFX pipelines, adapted to the specific demands of AI generation, and rather than revolving around individual prompts, the process began with the screenplay. The image pipeline combined Nano Banana 2, Flux 2 Pro, GPT Image 2 and Adobe Photoshop (Firefly) to generate original imagery; while video generation drew on Seedance 2, Seedance 2.5, Kling 3, Sora 2 Pro and Veo 3.1, with the model selected shot by shot according to the demands of each sequence. The entire audio component was developed through an ElevenLabs-based pipeline for voice synthesis and AI-assisted sound processing. Mieli describes the whole process as “fun” but serious and arduous as well. He stresses the lengths the production went to ensure an ethical approach in terms of the original elements used to generate the imagery and audio in the film. “It’s fun to play with, but it’s not really just a game; it has to be taken very seriously. We need to learn it, understand it, use it, change it, and master it, rather than letting AI master us,” he says. “We’ve actually worked toward an AI that aligns with what artists want, specifically ownership and creative control, rather than just focusing on rights and image ownership; essentially, all the issues people are rightly fighting for regarding AI.” As discussions get underway in Venice on the impact of AI on storytelling, Mieli says the film and TV world needs to take the bull by the horns. “The responsibility lies with us, the community of producers and directors, to study and understand it, and to see if we can build an AI that is fair and fosters a balanced relationship. But first and foremost, we need the curiosity to get to know it; you can’t talk about it without studying it.” ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments

title: Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom & Paramount International Boss Was 55
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse International Insider: Ciao, Venice; ‘Bake Off’ Battle Heats Up; Leslie Odom Jr. Chat Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom & Paramount International Boss Was 55 RTE’s ‘The Murder Of Mr. Moonlight’ To Explore Infamous Irish Killing; BBC & Banijay Rights On Board Drama Series View All September 4, 2026 1:25am Raffaelle Annecchino Blue Ocean Media Partners Raffaele Annecchino , the former international chief at Paramount and its predecessor Viacom, has died aged 55 from acute meningitis. The Italian executive, known for his negotiating skills and business acumen, passed away suddenly over the weekend while in the Balearic Islands, according to his personal office. The former President and CEO of Paramount International, Networks, Streaming and Studio, was a key figure in the rollouts of BET, MTV and Nickelodeon, and oversaw networks such as 5 in the UK and Ten in Australia. He is credited playing a major part in Paramount+’s international rollout, as well aiding the helping grow European SVoD SkyShowtime and free streamer Pluto TV. He was also on the boards Viacom 18 in India and SBS Media in South Korea. Related Stories News Gloria Steinem Dies: Feminist Icon And Activist & Co-Founder Of Ms. Magazine Was 92 News Jean-Paul Rappeneau Dies: 'Cyrano de Bergerac' Director Was 94 In total, Annecchino spent more than 25 years at Paramount/Viacom. He had originally joined the Madrid office in a commercial role and rose through the ranks. Further back, he worked at Warner Bros. Discovery predecessor Turner Broadcasting System for the likes of Cartoon Network and CNN. Watch on Deadline After leaving Paramount in 2022, he founded his own global media consultancy, Blue Ocean Media Partners, which he ran as President and CEO, with offices in Madrid and Dubai. Just this year, he joined Mediapro Middle East to provide strategic advice and support. “Raffaele Annecchino was much more than a boss to me,” wrote Blue Ocean partner Joana Carrion Boulos on LinkedIn. “He was one of those rare people who knew how to lead without making you feel that you were being led. He trusted the people he worked with, gave them space, listened to their ideas and, above all, made them feel valued.” “Such sad news,” wrote former Paramount President and CEO Bob Bakish, who worked closely with Annecchino for years, on social media. Raffa was a force of nature. Taken way too young. He will be missed by many. title: ‘Oasis’ Asks Uncomfortable Questions About Exclusion, and Its Director Explains Why Violence Is “Like a Virus”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 4, 2026 1:00am 'Oasis' Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion “Oasis” feels like a bit of a theme at Venice this year, with at least two movies featuring that word in their titles. One is Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern’s Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger , a documentary about the reunion tour of the famous English rock band. But it is the other film that could leave audiences truly rocked. Is a safe place simply a location or something we can create – a state of mind, even? German writer-director Jannis Lenz explores that and the various forms that exclusion and violence take in his feature debut Oasis ( Oase ). Related Stories Movies 'The End of Times' Is an AI-Assisted Film Essay on Trauma That Wants to "Politicize Mental Illness" (Exclusive Venice Trailer) Movies 'The Horsemen of the Apocalypse' Director Shares Insight Into Her Hybrid Movie That Revisits Her Filmmaker Father's Arrest and Death In the film, world-premiering on Sept. 6 in the Horizons section of the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival , a viral video of a student threatening his classmates surfaces online, causing concern among school staff, parents and kids. The student shown in the video and two other outcasts end up seeking refuge in a nearby forest. Their play turns into ritual, with pain becoming an escape. But then old wounds surface and, as notes on the film highlight, the boundaries between them are redrawn. Boundaries were fluid behind the scenes of the production. For example, Lenz directed Oasis based on a screenplay that he wrote with Alexander Dirninger, who also served as director of photography. Lenz also collaborated with Melisa Krasniqi in the editing process. The cast of Oasis is a showcase of established stars and up-and-coming German actors. Florian Geißelmann ( Sound of Falling , Home Stories ) as Lukas, Anton Petzold ( Home Stories , Ouija ) as Andrew and Mathilda Smidt ( Almania , Chabos ) as Maja feature as the young trio of outcasts, while veteran Godehard Giese plays one of their father’s and teacher ( Rose , Transit , Babylon Berlin ), with Britta Hammelstein ( Murder Mindfully , Woman of the Dead , The Sparrow in the Chimney ) potraying the school principal and Ioana Iacob ( Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World ) a school staff member. Oasis is produced by Germany’s Zeitgeist Filmproduktion and co-produced by Austria’s Wega Film and Germany’s Third Picture in collaboration with We Fade to Grey, Ocean Pictures Filmproduktion and Totem Films. The German theatrical release is planned for February 2027 via Mindjazz Pictures. Totem Films is handling international sales on the German-Austrian co-production. Lenz has also previously explored themes of the body and identity, as well as violence in his shorts, such as Shadowboxer (2015), Wannabe (2017), which was nominated for the European Film Award, and Soldat Ahmet (2021), which won several awards after its world premiere at the Visions du Réel festival in Switzerland. ‘Oasis’ Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion Ahead of the Venice world premiere of Oasis , Lenz talked to THR about the timely themes that his first feature, and his first film made after his return to Germany from Austria, dives into, exploring adolescent rage and pain in the digital age without providing easy answers, ensuring true collaboration with cast and crew, and casting Ahmet Simsek, who featured in two of his shorts. Thank you for the emotional, and at times difficult, film. Why did you want to make a film about the violent sides of adolescent and school life and beyond? I think that the stories that are probably the most uncomfortable to us are the ones that should be told. In this case, I moved back to Germany from Vienna, where I spent a third of my whole life. For family reasons, I moved back to the area where I grew up. And after so many years in the big city, I spent a lot of time in nature again, including in the woods where I played as a child – and now with my own children. The older one already goes to school, and so, through direct contact with the surroundings, so many memories came up again, and I felt I had to deal with them. In the end, we even ended up shooting in the same elementary school that I went to and that my son is now going to. When I grew up, there were school pressures, and there was the fear of ostracism. It seems like that is happening on a different level in our age of digital and social media. How do you think about how much has changed or stayed the same? When I was a teenager, it already started to go in this direction, but, of course, it was very different from what it is today. For example, my nephews and people in my very close surroundings and family [give me a chance] to talk and discuss these themes. I felt that it was something for kids that is always present in everything they do, in the way they think, in the way they behave. This feeling of always being watched is something that changes life. That was very important for me to explore because it will get more and more serious as my children are growing up, and so it will become a problem of mine too. Also, the thing about violence is, I think, that it just changes its form, but the problems remain the same. Now, it’s just on a digital level, and when I was young, it came in a more direct way. But it wasn’t better or worse. I think it’s just a different way that violence or pressure is coming to young people. Looking at the Netflix series Adolescence , it feels like adolescent rage and violence are particularly timely and universal topics… My aim was to get to the core of something, and in this case, it was how hierarchies are built in very early stages and the role models that shape us and that remain or stay with us for probably the rest of our lives. I think that happens very often in school. And I always try to make something as specific as possible, so that it becomes universal in the end. If you really get to the core of something, then many people can relate to it, and that was something I was aiming for. So, yes, violence and the things we describe is something that’s not specific to Austria or Germany – you find it in the whole world, because violence doesn’t stop at borders and it doesn’t make a difference between social classes and the like. It’s more like a virus that just changes its form and spreads. Oasis shows and touches on various types of violence, not just physical, but also verbal, non-verbal, social, etc. How early did you know you wanted to cover a range of violence? And violence is a theme that I have noticed you dive into throughout your shorts as well… Different views on violence are something that I’ve worked on in different films, especially in the films that I have worked on with Ahmet Simsek. In Shadowboxer , he was a young boxer forced into anti-violence training. Then I portrayed him in Soldat Ahmet in his job as a soldier in the barracks in the Austrian Federal Army and as a professional boxer. And now in Oasis , he’s holding an anti-violence training at the school. Jannis Lenz Courtesy of Béla Baptiste Your cast is such a great mix of established names and young up-and-comers. How was the casting process? I actually started from scratch because all my movies were made in Vienna up to this point, and so I didn’t know anybody in the German film scene. So I took a lot of time casting them. And because I come from the documentary side, this is something that shaped my work. So, I didn’t go into rehearsing scenes. It was more about coming together, talking, and getting to know each other, and trying to find out what we expect from the film and what the actors see in these characters, and then bringing the [core] three together and testing their chemistry. We brought together and mixed many young people in Berlin in a casting room, and things became absolutely clear. The chemistry between the three of them was so intense, and they felt it, and I felt it, and our casting director felt it. It was just clear that they must be this group that carries the film. The way you describe your process and your doc influence, I wonder how flexible the script was… I have a very concrete vision of how the film should be – what it should transport, and how it should feel. But the process to get there is open, and I am always in contact and in exchange, especially with my actors and what they bring in, because they are the ones who have to bring these characters from paper to life. My experience is that it is much better to give them space to bring in their own experiences than to push them to a point where they maybe don’t want to go. We were talking a lot for us to build trust. I felt that it needed this trust, and we had to build up the same safe place that the characters in the film are building for themselves. There is a scene that I won’t spoil with the three protagonists touching each other’s hands. In that and other scenes, Oasis felt very much like an all-around sensory experience to me. Does that make sense? Especially in this scene but also overall, we worked a lot with the sound design to make it a real experience for the audience. The changes are very subtle. But if you really dive into it, I think it’s a very special experience to let go like they let go. I saw that Benedikt Palier was in charge of the sound for Oasis , and I have come across his name repeatedly over the past year, for example, because he was also on the sound team of Sandra Wollner’s Everytime , among other films. I have worked with Benedikt for a long time. He also did the sound design for Soldat Ahmet , which was also very special. We both have the same way of working. We try to work with what is already in the film, rather than trying to invent things. We are working from the core of the storyline. Most of the sounds you actually hear are the starting point for the sound design, like a scene with a choir or guitar sounds, because there are guitars standing in Lukas’ room, and we have this one scene where [two characters are] playing Guitar Hero . So every sound is a starting point for the sound design, and then from the sound design, we build up to music. It’s a very organic process. Since we are talking about creative collaborators, I noticed that Alexander Dirninger is not only the cinematographer, but he also co-wrote the script with you, which seems rare. How did that come about? Well, Alexander and I studied together. We were in the same class at the Filmakademie Wien, and we knew that we wanted to make a project together. We were talking a lot about this project in a very early stage. And at a certain point, I felt it would be best just to write the script together because we already, from the very beginning, shared some visual ideas. I thought it would be uncommon but very fruitful to work with the DOP during the writing process because later on we also have to translate the written word into a film. It was a very, very inspiring collaboration. I can only recommend it. Did you feel that also helped the film feel like a really cohesive whole experience? Yeah, absolutely. In the end, the film should be bigger than the parts it’s built from. That develops out of people not only looking after their own department, but trying to build something together. And this is what filmmaking is for me. We tried to push this as far as possible in the system we’re working in to give several people more than just one position in the film, so that everything can merge together into something that’s bigger than the parts. The body is something that seems to fascinate you. Do you know where that interest comes from? Well, I started filmmaking with Parkour and Freerunning, filming my friends and myself during our training sessions, which was a very intuitive process. So nobody told me how to handle the camera or how to move or something like that. It was just filming and then editing it, before I even knew that I wanted to become a filmmaker. So my starting point was showing bodies in urban space, confronted with architecture and weightlessness and stuff like that. And so I think that definitely left traces. ‘Oasis’ Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion Given the heavy themes and difficult scenes that Oasis features, how did you guys deal with this on set and beyond? I was already in exchange with a psychologist during the process of writing, just because it’s a very sensitive subject, and I wanted to treat it seriously from the very beginning. And even before we started casting, we got in contact with an intimacy coordinator, and she was in dialogue with us during the casting process, and, of course, the rehearsals, and then on set. So we had rehearsals all together, where the young actors were building their choreographies together with the intimacy coordinator, and on set she was there every time there was a demanding scene. Of course, we were talking a lot about what this all means also on a psychological level because when we finish shooting, it’s not over. These are themes and topics that you have to deal with even after the camera is off, and we wanted to build the best safe space for them. How early did you find the title, Oasis ? Actually, it came very late. It was more like the conclusion of what we see in the film. This oasis in the film is not a place the three go to. It’s not a place in the landscape of the film. It’s something that exists in their mind, something they create for themselves, and that’s non-material. It was also very important for me to show the woods in the film. It’s not an idyllic place. It’s logged. There are wind turbines, which are louder than the birds, even in the last pockets where they hide. And so I didn’t want to romanticize this place, especially because in the German history context, the woods were used by the Nazis for propaganda issues – a sense of creating an image of belonging and identity, and I didn’t want to reproduce that in any way, not even unconsciously. So, the oasis is something they created for themselves. I won’t spoil the ending of the film, but you don’t let us off the hook easily… I knew from the very beginning that I didn’t want to end it with an easy answer that only pretends to be an answer. It’s such a complex topic, and it would have felt absolutely wrong. So what I felt what I had to do is to hand over the questions that stayed with me from my age as a teenager, to ask these questions as precisely as possible, and to leave the audience with these questions, not exactly knowing how to feel or what to think, but just to cope with them afterwards – and maybe feel “I have to talk about this with somebody else.” It’s also very important that the adults and the teachers were once also pupils going to school, and so that’s why I didn’t want to show them as the antagonists who do everything wrong, but just wanted to observe them with the same attentiveness with which I watch the teenagers and try to find out their motivations. In their case, their motivation is fear, and fear is never a good starting point for anything. THR

title: Louis Partridge & Anson Boon Set For British Coming-Of-Age Film ‘Andy & Orson’; MetFilm Launches Sales For TIFF Market
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Ron Perlman, Peter Facinelli & Mark Elias Starring In Indie Film ‘We Could Be Heroes’ Louis Partridge & Anson Boon Set For British Coming-Of-Age Film ‘Andy & Orson’; MetFilm Launches Sales For TIFF Market George Clooney Reveals The Rule He Tries To Live By, The Uncertain Path To Acting Success & His Next Movie — Venice Masterclass View All September 4, 2026 1:00am Louis Partridge and Anson Boon Keith Kandell/Getty EXCLUSIVE : Louis Partridge ( Enola Holmes ) and Anson Boon ( MobLand ) are set to star in Andy & Orson , the feature directorial debut of writer-directors Nathan Newman and Arnold T. Rice. MetFilm Sales is launching the project for worldwide sales ahead of the TIFF market with filming due to take place in the U.K. in early Q4, 2026. Brit actors Partridge and Boon will play the titular Andy and Orson, respectively, “two mismatched housemates whose friendship is tested over the course of a year as they navigate first heartbreaks, shifting ambitions and the messy realities of life in their twenties.” Related Stories News Aaron Eckhart, Brenton Thwaites & Bella Samman Leading Post-Apocalyptic Action Thriller 'Out Of The Ashes' -- TIFF Market News Josh Duhamel To Star In 'Speak' From Lorenzo Di Bonaventura & Joe Carnahan; Twenty-Nine Palms & CAA Media Finance Launching Sales At TIFF Set between South-East London and the British countryside, the film is described as “a contemporary story of friendship, love and growing up in the 2020s”. Watch on Deadline The film is produced by Jamie Clark and Aleksandra Bilić for My Accomplice, Dorottya Székely for Varga Pictures, and Carley Armstrong for True Moon Pictures. Executive producers are Newman and T. Rice through Tidewayout, Louis Partridge and Anson Boon, as well as Leopold Hughes ( Knives Out ). The movie is fully financed via the production companies and private investors and was developed by My Accomplice. Nathan Newman is the author of How to Leave the House , which was named a New Yorker Best Book of the Year, and which they later adapted for TV. Their second novel will be published next year. Arnold T. Rice is a social worker and independent filmmaker who frequently collaborates with UK comedians on viral sketches and stand-up specials. ‘’ Andy & Orson is about the highs and lows of being 20-somethings in the 2020s, written very deliberately throughout our own twenties in order to capture the shifts in ourselves and the decade. Like all great odd couples, we hope audiences see parts of themselves in both Andy and Orson when they hangout with them in theatres very soon,’’ said Newman and T. Rice. ‘’ Andy & Orson spoke to us in the rich tradition of odd couple, slacker films such as Clerks and Withnail and I. There is such a sharp contemporary edge to the script from Nathan and Arnold that will really connect with this generation of film fans. It’s testament to the script that we have talent such as Louis and Anson on board as leads,’’ added Jamie Clark, producer. Casting is currently underway for additional roles with the search led by casting director Claire Curry. Emmy-nominated cinematographer, Bart Sienkiewicz, is attached, along with costume designer Giulia Scrimieri, production designer Isabel Pirillo and hair and makeup designer Ziggy Gaji. Louis Partridge is represented by Independent Talent Group and WME. title: ‘Coming Of Age’: First Look At Josh Appignanesi’s Upcoming Comedy About “The Power Of Aging”
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Hit YouTube Series ‘Chicken Shop Date’ To End After 12-Year Run ‘Art Sex Music’: First Look At Caroline Catz’s Doc About British Artist & Musician Cosey Fanni Tutti ‘Bunker’: Watch Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz In Florian Zeller’s Venice-Bound Psychological Thriller View All September 3, 2026 11:28pm 'Coming of Age' Rob Baker Ashton EXCLUSIVE : Here’s a first look at writer-director Josh Appignanesi ’s seventh feature Coming of Age , which he co-wrote with longtime collaborator Devorah Baum . The film, which is told across 30 years of car rides through a fast-changing London, is described as a “heartfelt comedy about the power of aging”. It follows a couple navigating love, parenthood, midlife crises and aging parents, only to discover that getting older might just be the best part. The film stars Emun Elliott ( The Dark , The Gold ) as Jay and Lydia Wilson ( The Maids , Alice and Steve ) as Hannah, the couple at the heart of the story. Further cast include Peter Polycarpou ( The Brutalist , House of Dragon ) and Tristan Ruggeri ( The Twin , The Witcher ). Related Stories News RTE's 'The Murder Of Mr. Moonlight' To Explore Infamous Irish Killing; BBC & Banijay Rights On Board Drama Series Legal 'Criminal' Boss Ed Brubaker Accused Of Sexual & Racial Harassment; Amazon, MGM Also Named As Defendants In Complaint From Ex-PA Appignanesi ( Song of Songs ) and Baum’s script was inspired by research program ‘The Sciences of Aging and the Culture of Youth Project’, a program hosted at King’s College London which explores the concept of aging. The film, which was shot almost entirely on real roads, is produced by Emily Everdee for Lifelong Films, with Sam Buckler co-producing. Martina Zimmerman of SAACY is exec producer. It’s funded by UK Research and Innovation as part of SAACY. Watch on Deadline “Age is something we’re always faced with but can’t often bear to face,” said Appignanesi. “It makes fools of us, yet by the same token, deepens us. What would it look like to have the whole tragicomedy of a life reflected back to us in one arc? Might we walk away with something that helped us age a little better?” Baum added: “Coming-of-age stories tend to be about the journey from childhood into adolescence, while romantic comedies often end just as young people arrive at the altar. But what about the bit of life that comes afterwards? For most of us, that’s rather a lot of life. It’s also in midlife that age can start to feel impossible to ignore, in our bodies, our relationships, our sense of future possibilities…With Coming of Age , we wanted to move the happy ever after a little further down the road – to a point in life when audiences are less used to seeing it.” ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Sticks Lido Landing; Jack Huston & Lorenzo Mieli Interviews; More Raffaele Annecchino Dies: Former Viacom, Paramount Exec Was 55 Fox Orders Comedy Series ‘Mammoth’ From ‘Modern Family’ Duo Based On UK Format Maria Bartiromo Pink-Slipped From Fox After 12 Years: “Effective Today” Read More About: Comments
